pagetitle: "The Kaluza-Klein reduction"

# The Kaluza-Klein reduction {#sec-kk-reduction-group}

In 1921 Kaluza [@kaluza1921] observed that general relativity in five dimensions already contains electromagnetism. If the fifth
dimension is a circle and nothing depends on the position around it, the fifteen components of the
five-dimensional metric split into a four-dimensional metric, a vector field and a scalar, and the
five-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert action becomes four-dimensional gravity coupled to Maxwell's theory and to a
scalar field. The gauge field is a part of the geometry rather than an additional ingredient, and the gauge
symmetry is a coordinate change along the circle. Klein added in 1926 [@klein1926] that the circle must be very small, which
explains why it is not seen, and that the momentum around it is the electric charge. This idea, extended to
higher-dimensional internal spaces and to supergravity, runs through the rest of the tutorial.

The chapter carries out the reduction in full, in three sections. The first sets up the Kaluza-Klein ansatz: the
cylinder condition, the parametrisation of the metric by a four-dimensional metric $g_{\mu\nu}$, a vector $A_\mu$
and a scalar $\phi$, and the inverse and the determinant of the five-dimensional metric. The second computes the
Christoffel symbols, the Ricci tensor and the curvature scalar of the ansatz, the latter being
$\hat R = R + \tfrac14\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} - \tfrac{2}{\phi}\Box\phi$, and integrates the action over the circle.
The third removes the factor $\phi$ in front of the curvature by a Weyl rescaling of the metric, the passage from
the Jordan frame to the Einstein frame, and identifies the scalar as a dilaton whose value sets the strength of
the gauge coupling. The machinery is the Riemannian geometry of @sec-metrics and @sec-connections-curvature, the
Einstein-Hilbert action of @sec-general-relativity and the abelian gauge theory of @sec-gauge-theories, all in
the signature $(+, -, -, -)$ of @sec-conventions, extended to $(+, -, -, -, -)$ in five dimensions. Every
statement is followed by three examples and three exercises with hidden solutions; the curvature formulas are
polynomial identities in the values and derivatives of the fields at a point, and the explicit metrics are computed
with SageManifolds.

## Five-dimensional gravity and the Kaluza-Klein ansatz {#sec-kk-ansatz}

Kaluza's idea is to take the Einstein-Hilbert action of @sec-einstein-hilbert in five dimensions and to ask what a
four-dimensional observer sees when the fifth dimension is a small circle. Everything that follows is the geometry
of @sec-metrics applied to one $5 \times 5$ metric. This section sets up that metric, the Kaluza-Klein ansatz: the
cylinder condition, the identification of its components with a metric, a vector and a scalar on spacetime, its
inverse and its determinant. Our sources are @overduin1998 [Sec. 3] and @duff1994 [Secs. 1-2]; the conventions are
those of @sec-conventions, signature $(+, -, -, -, -)$ with the fifth coordinate $y$: the circle direction is spacelike,
so the internal block of the metric carries a minus sign (@sec-conventions-indices).

For more on this topic, see @emam2021covariant [Sec. 10.4] and @krasnov2020formulations [Sec. 2.6, Sec. 3.6].

### The cylinder condition

A metric on $M_4 \times S^1$ may depend on all five coordinates. Kaluza's first assumption removes the dependence on
the circle coordinate, so that the metric is in effect a collection of fields on four-dimensional spacetime. The
assumption has a geometric meaning, a symmetry of the metric, and a physical one, which Klein supplied.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-cylinder-condition}
#### Cylinder condition

A five-dimensional metric $\hat g_{AB}(x, y)$ on $M_4 \times S^1$ satisfies the **cylinder condition** if none of its
components depends on the circle coordinate, $\partial_y\hat g_{AB} = 0$. The vector field $\partial_y$ is then a Killing
vector (@def-killing), and the metric is determined by its components at a single value of $y$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Kaluza gave no reason for the condition. The first example records how Klein's periodic circle turns it from an
assumption into an approximation that becomes exact for small radii.

::: {#exm-cylinder-kaluza}
#### Kaluza's assumption

Kaluza imposed the condition by fiat, "for no good reason" as @duff1994 [p. 3] puts it; Klein explained it: on a
circle of radius $R$ every field is a Fourier series $\sum_nf_n(x)e^{iny/R}$, the mode $n$ has mass $|n|/R$
(@sec-kk-tower), and for small $R$ only the $y$-independent mode $n = 0$ is light.
:::

A two-dimensional version of the condition can be drawn. Its metric has one spacetime coordinate and one circle,
and it is the picture of the ansatz used throughout the chapter.

::: {#exm-cylinder-two-dimensions}
#### The two-dimensional toy

On the cylinder with coordinates $(x, y)$, $y \sim y + 2\pi$, the Riemannian metric $dx^2 + \phi(x)^2(dy + A(x)dx)^2$
satisfies the condition; it is the surface of revolution of radius $\phi(x)$ in @fig-kk-circle, and its curvature is
$R = -2\phi''/\phi$ whatever $A$ is (@exr-kk-toy). The toy is Riemannian so that it embeds as a surface; in the
five-dimensional ansatz below the $(x, y)$ block is $-dx^2 - \phi^2dy^2$ for flat $g$, its negative, and the
curvature changes sign (@exm-scalar-dilaton).
:::

The condition also has a precise meaning in terms of the Fourier modes. Setting the massive modes to zero is
consistent with the field equations, and this is what makes the four-dimensional theory a truncation rather than an
approximation.

::: {#exm-cylinder-zero-mode}
#### The zero-mode truncation

Keeping only $n = 0$ is a consistent truncation: the product of $y$-independent fields is $y$-independent, so the
zero modes never source the massive ones [@duff2025, p. 14]. The cylinder condition is thus the exact
statement that the massive Kaluza-Klein modes have been set to zero (@def-zero-mode-truncation).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The Kaluza-Klein ansatz in two dimensions, $ds^2 = dx^2 + \phi(x)^2(dy + A(x)dx)^2$: the surface of revolution
of radius $\phi(x)$ pictures the varying size of the circle, the gray circles are the fibres of constant $x$, and
the red curves are the horizontal curves $dy + A\,dx = 0$, closed where $A = 0$ (left) and winding where $A \neq 0$
(right). SageManifolds gives $R = -2\phi''/\phi$ independently of $A$. Generated by
`figures/kk_circle.sage`.](figures/kk_circle.svg){#fig-kk-circle width=85%}

{{< interactive kk_circle 460 >}}

The first exercise connects the condition with the Killing equation of @sec-flows-killing. It shows that the
condition is the coordinate form of a symmetry.

::: {#exr-kkr-cylinder-killing}
#### The Killing vector of the circle

Show that $\partial_y$ is a Killing vector of $\hat g$ if and only if $\partial_y\hat g_{AB} = 0$ in the coordinates
$(x^\mu, y)$, and that its flow $y \mapsto y + c$ maps each circle of constant $x$ into itself.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For a coordinate vector field the Lie derivative of the metric is the partial derivative of its components:
$(\mathcal{L}_{\partial_y}\hat g)_{AB} = \partial_y\hat g_{AB} + \hat g_{CB}\partial_A\delta^C_y + \hat g_{AC}\partial_B\delta^C_y =
\partial_y\hat g_{AB}$, since the components of $\partial_y$ are constant (@def-lie-derivative). The Killing equation
$\mathcal{L}_{\partial_y}\hat g = 0$ is therefore exactly the cylinder condition. The flow of $\partial_y$ is $(x, y)
\mapsto (x, y + c)$, which keeps $x$ fixed and rotates each circle rigidly.
:::

The two-dimensional toy of @exm-cylinder-two-dimensions hides its gauge field in a coordinate choice. The next
exercise removes it and computes the curvature, the statement drawn in @fig-kk-circle.

::: {#exr-kk-toy}
#### The two-dimensional ansatz

Show that the Riemannian toy $dx^2 + \phi(x)^2(dy + A(x)dx)^2$ is isometric to $dx^2 + \phi(x)^2dy'^2$ and compute its
curvature.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Put $y' = y + \int^xA$: then $dy' = dy + A\,dx$ and the metric is $dx^2 + \phi^2dy'^2$, the surface of revolution
with the induced metric of @def-induced-metric. Its Gaussian curvature is $K = -\phi''/\phi$ and $R = 2K = -2\phi''/\phi$
(@exm-gauss-sphere for the sign conventions), as SageManifolds confirms in `figures/kk_circle.sage` for the
original form with $A$ present. In two dimensions $A$ is pure gauge; in five it is not, because $F_{\mu\nu}$ need
not vanish. The dilaton example of @exm-scalar-dilaton has $\hat R = +2\phi''/\phi$: there the relevant block
$-dx^2 - \phi^2dy^2$ is the negative of the toy metric, and $R$ changes sign under $g \to -g$
(@sec-conventions-indices).
:::

The round sphere has a rotation symmetry, so it satisfies the cylinder condition in suitable coordinates. The second
exercise uses the two-dimensional curvature formula of @exm-cylinder-two-dimensions on it.

::: {#exr-kkr-cylinder-sphere}
#### The sphere as a toy

Write the round metric $d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2$ in the form of the toy of @exm-cylinder-two-dimensions,
identify $\phi$ and $A$, and compute its curvature from $R = -2\phi''/\phi$. Why does the toy description break down
at the poles?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $x = \theta$ and $y = \varphi$ the metric is $dx^2 + \phi(x)^2dy^2$ with $\phi = \sin\theta$ and $A = 0$, and it
satisfies the cylinder condition because no component depends on $\varphi$. Then $\phi'' = -\sin\theta$ and $R = -
2\phi''/\phi = 2$, the curvature of the unit sphere (@exm-gauss-sphere). At the poles $\phi = 0$: the circle shrinks
to a point, the fibration of the surface by circles is singular there, and the ansatz with $\phi > 0$ applies only
to the open cylinder $0 < \theta < \pi$.
:::

The third exercise makes the consistency of the zero-mode truncation concrete. It computes Fourier coefficients of
products of modes, which is how interactions between modes arise.

::: {#exr-kkr-cylinder-fourier}
#### Products of modes

Using the Fourier coefficients of @sec-fourier-series, show with Sage that a product of $y$-independent functions
has only a zero mode, that the product of the modes $e^{iy}$ and $e^{-iy}$ has a zero mode, and that $e^{iy}e^{iy}$
has only the mode $n = 2$. What does this say about truncating to the zero modes?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $n$-th coefficient of $e^{iay}e^{iby}$ is $\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{i(a + b - n)y}dy = \delta_{n, a + b}$: momentum
around the circle adds. Zero modes therefore generate only zero modes, so the equations for the massive modes are
solved by setting them to zero, while massive modes in pairs $(n, -n)$ do source the zero modes:

{{< sage exr-kkr-cylinder-fourier >}}

The truncation to $n = 0$ is consistent; the opposite truncation, dropping the zero modes, is not.
:::
::::

### The ansatz

A metric satisfying the cylinder condition has fifteen components that are functions on spacetime. The ansatz below
groups them into the fields a four-dimensional observer measures, in a way that makes their transformation laws
transparent; the essential step is to complete the square in $dy$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-ansatz}
#### Kaluza-Klein ansatz

The **Kaluza-Klein ansatz** is the five-dimensional metric
$$
d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}(x)\,dx^\mu dx^\nu - \phi(x)^2\left(dy + A_\mu(x)\,dx^\mu\right)^2 ,
$$ {#eq-kk-ansatz}
with components
$$
\hat g_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu} - \phi^2A_\mu A_\nu, \qquad \hat g_{\mu y} = -\phi^2A_\mu, \qquad \hat g_{yy} = -\phi^2 ,
$$ {#eq-kk-components}
all independent of $y$. It is the most general metric satisfying the cylinder condition, written so that its
fifteen components are a symmetric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$, a vector $A_\mu$ and a scalar $\phi > 0$ on $M_4$ [@overduin1998,
eq. 5, with $\kappa = 1$]. The minus sign makes the circle direction spacelike, so that $\hat g$ has signature
$(+, -, -, -, -)$ when $g$ has signature $(+, -, -, -)$, and the circumference of the circle over $x$ is $2\pi\phi(x)$.
The gauge coupling is restored in @sec-kk-tower.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The ansatz is easiest to manipulate as a block matrix. In this form its determinant and its inverse follow from the
block formulas of linear algebra.

::: {#exm-ansatz-matrix}
#### In block form

$\hat g = \begin{pmatrix} g - \phi^2AA^T & -\phi^2A \\ -\phi^2A^T & -\phi^2 \end{pmatrix}$: the $4 \times 4$ block, the
$4 \times 1$ column and the $1 \times 1$ corner. The index set is the disjoint union of the four spacetime indices and
the single circle index $y$ (@prp-kk-volume-factor).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The index set is $\text{Fin}\,4 \oplus \text{Unit}$, the summand $\text{Unit}$ being the circle direction, and
$\hat g$ is built with mathlib's `Matrix.fromBlocks` (`KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Gauge.det_ansatz`, @prp-kk-volume-factor).

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Switching off the vector leaves a metric in which only the size of the circle varies. It is the simplest
non-trivial case and already contains the scalar sector of the theory.

::: {#exm-ansatz-brans-dicke}
#### $A_\mu = 0$

$d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - \phi^2dy^2$, a warped product with the circle radius $\phi(x)$ varying over
spacetime; its reduction is the Brans-Dicke theory with $\omega = 0$ of @exm-jordan-brans-dicke [@overduin1998, Sec.
3.5].
:::

Switching off all variation gives the vacuum of the theory. Every later perturbative statement, such as the masses of
the Kaluza-Klein modes, refers to this background.

::: {#exm-ansatz-ground-state}
#### The ground state

$g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu}$, $A_\mu = 0$, $\phi = R$ constant: flat $M_4 \times S^1$ with a circle of radius $R$,
the vacuum around which the Fourier expansion of @sec-kk-tower is made [@duff1994, eq. 12].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise reads the components off the line element. It is the step from @eq-kk-ansatz to
@eq-kk-components, done by expanding the square.

::: {#exr-kkr-ansatz-components}
#### Reading off the components

Expand @eq-kk-ansatz and derive @eq-kk-components, remembering that the off-diagonal terms $\hat g_{\mu y}dx^\mu dy$
appear twice in $\hat g_{AB}dx^Adx^B$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$(dy + A_\mu dx^\mu)^2 = dy^2 + 2A_\mu dx^\mu dy + A_\mu A_\nu dx^\mu dx^\nu$, so $d\hat s^2 = (g_{\mu\nu} - \phi^2A_\mu
A_\nu)dx^\mu dx^\nu - 2\phi^2A_\mu dx^\mu dy - \phi^2dy^2$. Comparing with $\hat g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu + 2\hat g_{\mu y}dx^\mu dy +
\hat g_{yy}dy^2$ gives $\hat g_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu} - \phi^2A_\mu A_\nu$, $\hat g_{\mu y} = -\phi^2A_\mu$ and $\hat g_{yy} = -\phi^2$.
Conversely every symmetric $\hat g$ with $\hat g_{yy} < 0$ is of this form: $\phi^2 = -\hat g_{yy}$, $A_\mu = \hat
g_{\mu y}/\hat g_{yy}$, $g_{\mu\nu} = \hat g_{\mu\nu} + \phi^2A_\mu A_\nu$.
:::

The scalar $\phi$ measures the size of the circle. The second exercise makes this precise with the length of a
curve, @sec-metrics.

::: {#exr-kkr-ansatz-circumference}
#### The size of the circle

Compute the proper length of the closed curve $y \mapsto (x_0, y)$, $0 \leq y \leq 2\pi$, in the metric
@eq-kk-ansatz. Does it depend on $A_\mu$? Is the curve a geodesic when $\phi$ is not constant?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The tangent vector is $\partial_y$, with $\hat g(\partial_y, \partial_y) = -\phi^2 < 0$ (spacelike), so the length is
$\int_0^{2\pi}\sqrt{|\hat g_{yy}|}\,dy = 2\pi\phi(x_0)$, independently of $A_\mu$. The geodesic equation for $x^\lambda$
along the curve is $\ddot x^\lambda + \hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy}\dot y^2 = 0$ with $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy} = \phi\partial^\lambda\phi$
(@eq-kk-christoffel), so the circle is a geodesic only where $\partial\phi = 0$: otherwise a curve along the fibre is
pushed towards larger circles (@exm-christoffel-upper-spacetime).
:::

The signature of the ansatz was asserted in the definition. The third exercise proves it by writing the metric as a
congruence transformation of a block-diagonal matrix.

::: {#exr-kkr-ansatz-signature}
#### The signature

Let $E$ be the $5 \times 5$ matrix whose rows are the components of the one-forms $dx^\mu$ and $e^y = dy +
A_\mu dx^\mu$. Show that $\hat g = E^T\operatorname{diag}(g, -\phi^2)E$, and deduce with Sylvester's law of inertia that
$\hat g$ has signature $(+, -, -, -, -)$. Check with a numerical example.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$d\hat s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - \phi^2(e^y)^2$ is the statement $\hat g = E^T\operatorname{diag}(g, -\phi^2)E$, and $E$ is
lower triangular with unit diagonal, so $\det E = 1$. Congruent symmetric matrices have the same numbers of positive
and negative eigenvalues, so $\hat g$ has the signature of $g$ plus one minus sign:

{{< sage exr-kkr-ansatz-signature >}}
:::
::::

The ansatz gives names to the components, but names are justified by transformation laws. The next definition states
how the three fields behave under the coordinate changes that preserve the form of the ansatz and do not touch the
circle.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-fields}
#### The Kaluza-Klein fields

Under a four-dimensional coordinate change $x \mapsto x'(x)$ at fixed $y$, which is a five-dimensional coordinate
change with $\xi^y = 0$, the components @eq-kk-components transform so that $g_{\mu\nu}$ is a tensor
(@def-tensor-field), $A_\mu$ a covector (@def-one-form) and $\phi$ a scalar: the **Kaluza-Klein fields** are a
metric, a gauge field and a scalar on spacetime [@duff1994, eq. 9].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The transformation laws follow from the tensor law of the five-dimensional metric. The first example sketches the
argument, which @exr-kk-tensor-law completes.

::: {#exm-fields-tensor-law}
#### From the five-dimensional tensor law

$\hat g'_{AB} = \frac{\partial x^C}{\partial x'^A}\frac{\partial x^D}{\partial x'^B}\hat g_{CD}$ with
$\partial y/\partial x'^\mu = 0$ gives $\hat g'_{yy} = \hat g_{yy}$, so $\phi$ is a scalar; $\hat g'_{\mu y} = \frac{\partial x^\nu}
{\partial x'^\mu}\hat g_{\nu y}$, so $-\phi^2A_\mu$ and hence $A_\mu$ is a covector; and then $g_{\mu\nu} = \hat g_{\mu\nu} +
\phi^2A_\mu A_\nu$ is a tensor (@exr-kk-tensor-law).
:::

A reparametrisation of fields must not lose information. Counting components confirms that the three fields are
exactly as many functions as the metric they replace.

::: {#exm-fields-counting}
#### Counting components

$10 + 4 + 1 = 15$, the components of a symmetric $5 \times 5$ matrix: nothing is lost or added, and the three
fields are precisely the massless spin-$2$, spin-$1$ and spin-$0$ zero modes of @def-zero-mode-truncation
[@duff1994, p. 11].
:::

The four-dimensional coordinate changes are not the only ones that preserve the ansatz. The third example looks at
the remaining one, which is the subject of the next chapter.

::: {#exm-fields-y-shift}
#### The remaining coordinate freedom

A coordinate change with $\xi^y = \epsilon(x)$ keeps the form @eq-kk-ansatz but shifts $A_\mu$ by $-\partial_\mu\epsilon$:
this is the gauge transformation of @sec-kk-gauge, the reason $A_\mu$ is a gauge field and not just a covector.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise carries out the derivation of the transformation laws in full. It needs only the block structure
of the Jacobian.

::: {#exr-kk-tensor-law}
#### The tensor law

Verify from $\hat g'_{AB} = \frac{\partial x^C}{\partial x'^A}\frac{\partial x^D}{\partial x'^B}\hat g_{CD}$ with $x' = x'(x)$,
$y' = y$ that $g_{\mu\nu}$, $A_\mu$, $\phi$ transform as a tensor, a covector and a scalar.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Jacobian is block diagonal, $\partial x^\nu/\partial x'^\mu = J^\nu{}_\mu$ and $\partial y/\partial y' = 1$. Then $\hat g'_{yy}
= \hat g_{yy}$ gives $\phi' = \phi$; $\hat g'_{\mu y} = J^\nu{}_\mu\hat g_{\nu y}$ gives $-\phi^2A'_\mu = -J^\nu{}_\mu\phi^2A_\nu$, the
covector law; and $\hat g'_{\mu\nu} = J^\rho{}_\mu J^\sigma{}_\nu\hat g_{\rho\sigma}$ gives $g'_{\mu\nu} - \phi^2A'_\mu A'_\nu =
J^\rho{}_\mu J^\sigma{}_\nu(g_{\rho\sigma} - \phi^2A_\rho A_\sigma)$, whose $AA$ terms agree by the covector law, leaving the
tensor law for $g$ (@def-tensor-field).
:::

A Lorentz boost is a four-dimensional coordinate change, so it must act on the Kaluza-Klein fields as on a metric, a
covector and a scalar. The second exercise checks this on a concrete boost.

::: {#exr-kkr-fields-boost}
#### A boost at fixed $y$

Take $g = \eta$, a constant $A_\mu$ and a constant $\phi$, and apply the boost $t = \cosh b\,t' + \sinh b\,x'$, $x =
\sinh b\,t' + \cosh b\,x'$, $y' = y$. Show with Sage that the transformed ansatz has $g' = \eta$, $A' = \Lambda^TA$
and $\phi' = \phi$, where $\Lambda$ is the boost matrix.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Jacobian is $\operatorname{diag}(\Lambda, 1)$ and $\Lambda^T\eta\Lambda = \eta$, so the $AA^T$ term becomes
$(\Lambda^TA)(\Lambda^TA)^T$ and the column $-\phi^2A$ becomes $-\phi^2\Lambda^TA$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-fields-boost >}}

An electric potential $A_0$ acquires a component $A_1 = A_0\sinh b$ in the moving frame, as a four-vector potential
must.
:::

The counting of @exm-fields-counting generalises to any number of dimensions. The third exercise does the count and
compares the number of degrees of freedom of the massless fields.

::: {#exr-kkr-fields-count}
#### Counting in $d + 1$ dimensions

Count the components of a metric in $d + 1$ dimensions satisfying the cylinder condition and split them into a
$d$-dimensional metric, a vector and a scalar. For $d = 4$, how many physical polarisations do the massless graviton,
photon and scalar carry, and how many does a five-dimensional graviton carry?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac12(d + 1)(d + 2) = \tfrac12d(d + 1) + d + 1$: a symmetric $d \times d$ matrix, a $d$-vector and a scalar. For
$d = 4$: $15 = 10 + 4 + 1$. The physical polarisations of a massless graviton in $D$ dimensions number
$\tfrac12D(D - 3)$, $2$ for $D = 4$ and $5$ for $D = 5$; the photon in four dimensions has $2$ and the scalar $1$, so
$2 + 2 + 1 = 5$: the five-dimensional graviton is exactly the four-dimensional graviton, photon and scalar, as
@exm-fields-counting says at the level of components.
:::
::::

### Inverse and determinant

Curvature computations need the inverse metric, and the action needs the volume element. Both are simple for the
ansatz, because completing the square in @eq-kk-ansatz has already diagonalised the metric in a frame; the inverse
is stated first.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-inverse-metric}
#### Inverse of the ansatz metric

The inverse of @eq-kk-components is
$$
\hat g^{\mu\nu} = g^{\mu\nu}, \qquad \hat g^{\mu y} = -A^\mu, \qquad \hat g^{yy} = -\phi^{-2} + A_\mu A^\mu ,
$$ {#eq-kk-inverse}
with $A^\mu = g^{\mu\nu}A_\nu$ (@prp-kk-inverse): the inverse of the four-dimensional metric sits in the spacetime
block, and the $A$-dependence moves to the mixed and corner entries.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The inverse can be checked by multiplying out. The first example does the three block products, which use nothing but
$g^{\mu\lambda}g_{\lambda\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nu$.

::: {#exm-inverse-check}
#### Checking $\hat g^{AC}\hat g_{CB} = \delta^A_B$

$\hat g^{\mu\lambda}\hat g_{\lambda\nu} + \hat g^{\mu y}\hat g_{y\nu} = g^{\mu\lambda}(g_{\lambda\nu} - \phi^2A_\lambda A_\nu) + A^\mu\phi^2A_\nu
= \delta^\mu_\nu$, $\hat g^{\mu\lambda}\hat g_{\lambda y} + \hat g^{\mu y}\hat g_{yy} = -\phi^2A^\mu + \phi^2A^\mu = 0$, and
$\hat g^{y\lambda}\hat g_{\lambda y} + \hat g^{yy}\hat g_{yy} = \phi^2A^\lambda A_\lambda + 1 - \phi^2A_\lambda A^\lambda = 1$
(@exr-kk-inverse-metric).
:::

At the ground state the inverse is diagonal. The second example shows that its circle entry is what produces the
Kaluza-Klein masses.

::: {#exm-inverse-ground-state}
#### At the ground state

With $A = 0$, $\hat g^{AB} = \operatorname{diag}(g^{\mu\nu}, -\phi^{-2})$, and at $\phi = R$ the circle direction is
rescaled by $-R^{-2}$: on the mode $e^{iny}$ (period $2\pi$ in $y$) the operator $\hat g^{yy}\partial_y^2$ gives
$-R^{-2}\cdot(-n^2) = (n/R)^2$, so $\hat g^{AB}\partial_A\partial_B = \Box_4 + (n/R)^2$, the origin of the mass
$|n|/R$ (@sec-kk-tower).
:::

In the curvature computations of @sec-kk-reduction the inverse of the four-dimensional metric is not computed but
treated as a set of new variables. The third example explains why this is enough.

::: {#exm-inverse-free-symbols}
#### The inverse as free symbols

In the jet computations of @sec-kk-reduction the entries $g^{\mu\nu}$ are independent symbols and @eq-kk-inverse is
the definition of $\hat g^{AB}$; the reduction never needs $g^{\mu\lambda}g_{\lambda\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nu$, a fact the
computation itself reveals (@def-jet-variables).
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The statements of `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Jets` take the entries $g^{\mu\nu}$ as free variables and define
$\hat g^{AB}$ by @eq-kk-inverse; they are proved by `ring` without any lemma about the inverse (@prp-kk-scalar).

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise multiplies out the inverse symbolically, with a completely general four-dimensional metric. It
is the computation behind @prp-kk-inverse.

::: {#exr-kk-inverse-metric}
#### The inverse metric in Sage

Build the ansatz as a block matrix with a generic symmetric $g$ and verify @eq-kk-inverse and @eq-kk-volume.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kk-inverse-metric >}}
:::

The two-dimensional toy has an inverse that can be written out by hand. The second exercise compares it with the
general formula.

::: {#exr-kkr-inverse-toy}
#### The inverse of the toy metric

Invert the $2 \times 2$ matrix of the Riemannian toy $dx^2 + \phi^2(dy + A\,dx)^2$ directly, and compare with
@eq-kk-inverse after the sign changes $g = 1$, $-\phi^2 \to \phi^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The matrix is $\begin{pmatrix} 1 + \phi^2A^2 & \phi^2A \\ \phi^2A & \phi^2 \end{pmatrix}$ with determinant $\phi^2$, so its
inverse is $\phi^{-2}\begin{pmatrix} \phi^2 & -\phi^2A \\ -\phi^2A & 1 + \phi^2A^2 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -A \\ -A &
\phi^{-2} + A^2 \end{pmatrix}$. @eq-kk-inverse with $g^{xx} = 1$ and $\phi^2$ replaced by $-\phi^2$ gives $\hat g^{xx} = 1$,
$\hat g^{xy} = -A$, $\hat g^{yy} = \phi^{-2} + A^2$: the same matrix.
:::

The inverse metric raises indices, and the frame in which the ansatz is diagonal has a dual frame of vectors. The
third exercise finds it by raising the indices of the frame one-forms.

::: {#exr-kkr-inverse-dual-frame}
#### The dual frame

Show with Sage that $\hat g^{AB}$ maps the one-form $e^y = dy + A_\mu dx^\mu$ to the vector $-\phi^{-2}\partial_y$ and $dx^\mu$
to $g^{\mu\nu}h_\nu$, where $h_\nu = \partial_\nu - A_\nu\partial_y$. What is $\hat g^{AB}$ in the frame $(h_\mu, \partial_y)$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Raising with @eq-kk-inverse, with $g^{\mu\nu}$ as free symbols:

{{< sage exr-kkr-inverse-dual-frame >}}

So the vectors dual to $(dx^\mu, e^y)$ are $(h_\mu, \partial_y)$, and in this frame $\hat g^{AB} = \operatorname{diag}(g^{\mu\nu}, -
\phi^{-2})$: written in the frame, the inverse ansatz is as simple as the ansatz itself.
:::
::::

The determinant of the ansatz controls the volume element of the five-dimensional action. Its simplicity is the first
sign that the vector field enters the reduced theory only through its field strength.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-volume-factor}
#### Volume factor

The determinant of the ansatz metric is $\det\hat g = -\phi^2\det g$, positive since $\det g < 0$ (with four spacelike
directions the determinant of a five-dimensional Lorentzian metric is positive), so the five-dimensional volume
element is
$$
\sqrt{|\hat g|}\,d^5x = \phi\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x\,dy ,
$$ {#eq-kk-volume}
the four-dimensional volume element times the circumference factor $\phi$ (@prp-kk-volume-factor).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The block-determinant formula of linear algebra computes the determinant in one line. The first example applies it
and shows how the vector drops out.

::: {#exm-volume-block}
#### By the block determinant

$\det\begin{pmatrix} P & Q \\ Q^T & D \end{pmatrix} = \det D\,\det(P - QD^{-1}Q^T)$ with $D = -\phi^2$, $Q = -\phi^2A$ gives
$-\phi^2\det(g - \phi^2AA^T + \phi^2AA^T) = -\phi^2\det g$: the $A$-dependence cancels exactly. This is the proof
of @prp-kk-volume-factor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Gauge.det_ansatz` is proved by this Schur-complement argument, with mathlib's
determinant formula for `Matrix.fromBlocks` with an invertible corner.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

In two dimensions the volume element is an area element and can be seen on the surface of revolution. The second
example computes it.

::: {#exm-volume-two-dimensions}
#### The toy model

For the Riemannian toy $dx^2 + \phi^2(dy + A\,dx)^2$, $\det = (1 + \phi^2A^2)\phi^2 - \phi^4A^2 = \phi^2$: the area
element is $\phi\,dx\,dy$, the circumference $2\pi\phi(x)$ times $dx$, as the surface of revolution of @fig-kk-circle
shows. With the circle block negative, $dx^2 - \phi^2(dy + A\,dx)^2$, the determinant is $-\phi^2$ and the area
element $\sqrt{|\det|}\,dx\,dy$ is again $\phi\,dx\,dy$.
:::

The volume factor enters the action directly. The third example shows the consequence for the reduced Lagrangian. It explains where the scalar factor in the reduced Lagrangian comes from.

::: {#exm-volume-action}
#### In the action

$\int d^5x\sqrt{|\hat g|}\,\hat R = \int dy\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,\phi\hat R$: after the $y$-integral the reduced Lagrangian
carries an overall $\phi$, the origin of the Jordan-frame form of @sec-kk-einstein-frame.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes an area with the volume factor. The surface is the one of @fig-kk-circle, so the result
can be compared with elementary geometry.

::: {#exr-kkr-volume-toy-area}
#### The area of the toy surface

Compute the area of the part $-3 \leq x \leq 3$ of the surface $dx^2 + \phi(x)^2(dy + A(x)dx)^2$ with $\phi = 1 + 0.
35\sin x$ and any $A$, and compare with the lateral area of a cylinder of radius $1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The area element is $\phi\,dx\,dy$ by @exm-volume-two-dimensions, so the area is $\int_{-3}^3\int_0^{2\pi}\phi\,dy\,dx =
2\pi\int_{-3}^3(1 + 0.35\sin x)dx = 2\pi \cdot 6 = 12\pi$, because $\sin$ is odd. This is the lateral area of the
cylinder of radius $1$ and length $6$, and it does not depend on $A$: the bulges and the necks of the surface
compensate. (The induced metric of the embedded surface of revolution is $(1 + \phi'^2)dx^2 + \phi^2dy^2$, whose area is
larger; the toy metric is not that induced metric, only pictured by it.)
:::

The cancellation of $A$ in the determinant is not special to four dimensions. The second exercise checks it in every
dimension up to four with Sage.

::: {#exr-kkr-volume-dims}
#### Every dimension

Show that the $(d + 1) \times (d + 1)$ ansatz built from a symmetric $d \times d$ matrix $g$, a $d$-vector $A$ and
$\phi$ has determinant $-\phi^2\det g$, for $d = 1, 2, 3, 4$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The block-determinant argument of @exm-volume-block does not use $d = 4$. Sage confirms the polynomial identity:

{{< sage exr-kkr-volume-dims >}}
:::

The circle integral in the action depends on the period chosen for $y$. The third exercise makes the bookkeeping
explicit, which matters when comparing conventions.

::: {#exr-kkr-volume-circle}
#### Integrating over the circle

For a $y$-independent function $f(x)$, compute $\int d^5x\sqrt{|\hat g|}\,f$ when $y \sim y + 2\pi$, and when $y \sim y +
2\pi L$. Show that the coordinate $y' = y/L$ turns the second ansatz into the first with $(\phi, A)$ replaced by $(L\phi,
A/L)$, and conclude which combination of $\phi$ and the period is physical.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With period $2\pi$ the integral is $2\pi\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,\phi f$, and with period $2\pi L$ it is $2\pi L\int
d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,\phi f$. With $y = Ly'$, $\phi^2(dy + A_\mu dx^\mu)^2 = (L\phi)^2(dy' + L^{-1}A_\mu dx^\mu)^2$ and $y'$ has period
$2\pi$: the same metric is the ansatz for $(g, A/L, L\phi)$, and $2\pi\int\sqrt{-g}\,(L\phi)f$ agrees with the second
integral. Only the circumference, period times $\phi$, is physical; this is why @sec-kk-tower can use $y \sim y + 2\pi R$
with $\phi = 1$ in place of $y \sim y + 2\pi$ with $\phi = R$, at the price of rescaling $A$.
:::
::::

The two propositions of this section state the inverse and the determinant as identities. The first holds for a
completely general symmetric four-dimensional metric.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kk-inverse}
#### The inverse metric

$\hat g^{AC}\hat g_{CB} = \delta^A_B$ for @eq-kk-inverse with a generic symmetric four-dimensional metric, and
$\det\hat g = -\phi^2\det g$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A constant gauge field in flat space gives a concrete inverse. The first example writes it out and shows the role of
the signature in raising the index of $A$.

::: {#exm-kkr-inverse-constant-field}
#### A constant potential

For $g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$ and $A = (0, a, 0, 0)$, $A^\mu = \eta^{\mu\nu}A_\nu = (0, -a, 0, 0)$, so $\hat g^{xy} = -A^x = a$ and
$\hat g^{yy} = -1 + A_\mu A^\mu = -1 - a^2$. The corner entry is more negative than at the ground state: a spacelike
potential makes the inverse metric lean further into the circle direction.
:::

The entries of the inverse are polynomials once $g^{\mu\nu}$ and $\phi^{-1}$ are given. The second example explains
why this turns the proposition into a finite algebraic identity.

::: {#exm-kkr-inverse-polynomial}
#### Polynomial entries

Every entry of @eq-kk-inverse is a polynomial in $g^{\mu\nu}$, $A_\mu$ and $\phi^{-2}$; the only division is the one hidden
in $g^{\mu\nu}$. The product $\hat g^{AC}\hat g_{CB}$ is then a polynomial that reduces to $\delta^A_B$ modulo
$g^{\mu\lambda}g_{\lambda\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nu$ and $\phi^{-2}\phi^2 = 1$, so the inverse is established by polynomial
algebra alone, without solving any equation.
:::

At the ground state both statements of the proposition are elementary. The third example states them as a sanity
check of the signs.

::: {#exm-kkr-inverse-ground-determinant}
#### The ground state

For $\eta_{\mu\nu}$, $A = 0$, $\phi = R$, $\hat g = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1, -R^2)$, $\det\hat g = R^2 = -R^2\det\eta$
(with $\det\eta = -1$), and $\hat g^{-1} = \operatorname{diag}(1, -1, -1, -1, -R^{-2})$, in agreement with @eq-kk-inverse.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the inverse rather than verifying it. It uses the Schur complement, the same tool as
@exm-volume-block.

::: {#exr-kkr-inverse-schur}
#### Deriving the inverse

Use the block inversion formula $\begin{pmatrix} P & Q \\ Q^T & D \end{pmatrix}^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} S^{-1} & -S^{-1}QD^{-1}
\\ -D^{-1}Q^TS^{-1} & D^{-1} + D^{-1}Q^TS^{-1}QD^{-1} \end{pmatrix}$, $S = P - QD^{-1}Q^T$, to derive @eq-kk-inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $P = g - \phi^2AA^T$, $Q = -\phi^2A$, $D = -\phi^2$: $QD^{-1}Q^T = -\phi^2AA^T$, so $S = g$ and $S^{-1} = g^{-1}$.
Then $-S^{-1}QD^{-1} = -g^{-1}(-\phi^2A)(-\phi^{-2}) = -g^{-1}A$, which is $\hat g^{\mu y} = -A^\mu$, and $D^{-1} +
D^{-1}Q^TS^{-1}QD^{-1} = -\phi^{-2} + \phi^{-4}\phi^4A^Tg^{-1}A = -\phi^{-2} + A_\mu A^\mu$. The Schur complement being $g$
itself is the algebraic form of completing the square in @eq-kk-ansatz.
:::

The horizontal lifts of @exr-kkr-inverse-dual-frame are orthogonal to the circle. The second exercise verifies this
and the inner products of the lifts with Sage.

::: {#exr-kkr-horizontal-lift}
#### Horizontal lifts

Show that $h_\mu = \partial_\mu - A_\mu\partial_y$ satisfies $\hat g(h_\mu, \partial_y) = 0$ and $\hat g(h_\mu, h_\nu) = g_{\mu\nu}$, and
interpret: what does a four-dimensional observer measure with $g_{\mu\nu}$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Direct evaluation with the components @eq-kk-components:

{{< sage exr-kkr-horizontal-lift >}}

So $g_{\mu\nu}$ measures the displacements orthogonal to the circle: the distance between two nearby circles is
computed with $g$ along the horizontal directions, and $g$ is the metric induced on the space of circles (the
quotient by the $U(1)$ action), not the metric induced on a slice $y = \text{const}$, which is $\hat g_{\mu\nu} = g -
\phi^2AA$.
:::

The proposition assumes that the inverse exists. The third exercise asks when it does. The answer shows that only the circle itself can degenerate.

::: {#exr-kkr-inverse-degenerate}
#### When is the ansatz invertible?

Using @eq-kk-volume, find the conditions on $g$, $A$ and $\phi$ under which $\hat g$ is invertible. Can a large $A$ make
the ansatz degenerate?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\det\hat g = -\phi^2\det g$ vanishes exactly when $\phi = 0$ or $\det g = 0$, whatever $A$ is: no gauge field, however
large, makes the ansatz degenerate. At $\phi = 0$ the circle shrinks to a point and the ansatz is singular, as at the
poles of @exr-kkr-cylinder-sphere; the inverse @eq-kk-inverse indeed contains $\phi^{-2}$.
:::
::::

The second proposition is the determinant identity alone, for an arbitrary square block. It is stated for the block
matrix of @exm-ansatz-matrix, with no symmetry assumed.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kk-volume-factor}
#### The volume factor

$\det\hat g = -\phi^2\det g$ for the block matrix of @exm-ansatz-matrix and any $4 \times 4$ matrix $g$, when $\phi \neq
0$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The proposition splits the index set into spacetime and circle indices. The first example explains this splitting,
which keeps the two kinds of index apart and reduces the determinant to a block formula.

::: {#exm-kkr-volume-index-set}
#### The index set

The rows and columns of $\hat g$ are indexed by the disjoint union $\{0, 1, 2, 3\} \sqcup \{y\}$: an index is either a
spacetime index $\mu$ or the circle index $y$. Splitting the index set this way writes $\hat g = \begin{pmatrix} P & Q \\ Q^T
& D \end{pmatrix}$ with $P = g - \phi^2AA^T$, $Q = -\phi^2A$ and $D = -\phi^2$, and the Schur-complement formula
$\det\hat g = \det D\,\det(P - QD^{-1}Q^T)$, valid when the corner $D$ is invertible, gives the determinant.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The index set is `Fin 4 ⊕ Unit`: an index is either `inl μ` with $\mu \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ or `inr ()`, the
circle. Mathlib's `Matrix.fromBlocks` builds $\hat g$ from its four blocks, and the Schur-complement lemma for
`fromBlocks` with an invertible corner gives the determinant (`KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Gauge.det_ansatz`).

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The statement holds for any $4 \times 4$ matrix, not only for symmetric ones. The second example comments on this
generality.

::: {#exm-kkr-volume-any-matrix}
#### Any matrix

Neither symmetry nor signature is used: the identity is a polynomial identity in the sixteen entries of $g$, the four
of $A$ and $\phi$. A proof of the general identity is simpler than one restricted to metrics, because no hypothesis has
to be carried along (@exr-kkr-volume-nonsym).
:::

The hypothesis $\phi \neq 0$ comes from the proof, not from the identity. The third example looks at the excluded
case.

::: {#exm-kkr-volume-degenerate}
#### $\phi = 0$

At $\phi = 0$ the ansatz is $\operatorname{diag}(g, 0)$ and both sides vanish, so the identity still holds; the hypothesis
is needed only because the Schur complement divides by the corner $-\phi^2$. The polynomial identity of
@exr-kkr-volume-nonsym holds without it.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise confirms the generality claimed in @exm-kkr-volume-any-matrix. It expands the determinant of a
fully generic block matrix. Sage expands both sides as polynomials in all the entries.

::: {#exr-kkr-volume-nonsym}
#### A non-symmetric block

Verify with Sage that $\det\hat g = -\phi^2\det g$ for a $4 \times 4$ matrix $g$ with sixteen independent entries.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kkr-volume-nonsym >}}

The identity holds as polynomials, including at $\phi = 0$.
:::

A determinant is unchanged by adding multiples of one column to another. The second exercise gives a proof of the
volume factor with column operations, without the Schur complement.

::: {#exr-kkr-volume-columns}
#### By column operations

Subtract $A_\nu$ times the last column of $\hat g$ from its column $\nu$, for each $\nu$, then do the analogous row
operations, and read off $\det\hat g$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Subtracting $A_\nu$ times the last column $(-\phi^2A_\mu, -\phi^2)^T$ from column $\nu$ changes the $(\mu, \nu)$ entry to
$g_{\mu\nu} - \phi^2A_\mu A_\nu + \phi^2A_\mu A_\nu = g_{\mu\nu}$ and the $(y, \nu)$ entry to $-\phi^2A_\nu + \phi^2A_\nu = 0$; subtracting
$A_\mu$ times the last row from row $\mu$ then clears the entries $(\mu, y)$. Together these operations are the congruence
by $E^{-1}$ of @exr-kkr-ansatz-signature. The result is $\operatorname{diag}(g, -\phi^2)$, the operations do not
change the determinant, and $\det\hat g = -\phi^2\det g$.
:::

The volume element takes the square root of the determinant. The third exercise checks the sign conventions that
make it equal to $\phi\sqrt{-g}$.

::: {#exr-kkr-volume-sqrt}
#### The square root

Show that $\sqrt{|\det\hat g|} = |\phi|\sqrt{-\det g}$ and explain why the text may write $\phi\sqrt{-g}$. What changes
for a Riemannian $g$ with the toy sign $+\phi^2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|\det\hat g| = \phi^2|\det g| = \phi^2(-\det g)$ for Lorentzian $g$, whose determinant is negative, so $\sqrt{|\hat g|} = |
\phi|\sqrt{-g}$, and $|\phi| = \phi$ because the ansatz takes $\phi > 0$ (the sign of $\phi$ is invisible in
@eq-kk-ansatz, which contains only $\phi^2$). For a Riemannian $g$ and the toy sign the determinant is $+\phi^2\det g > 0$
and $\sqrt{\det} = \phi\sqrt{\det g}$, as in @exm-volume-two-dimensions.
:::
::::

## The reduction of the curvature scalar {#sec-kk-reduction}

The computation at the heart of Kaluza-Klein theory is the curvature scalar of the ansatz metric, which turns out
to be the four-dimensional one plus a Maxwell term and a term in the scalar. This section carries it out in full,
one tensor at a time with the definitions of @sec-connections-curvature: the Christoffel symbols, the Ricci tensor
and the scalar, each displayed as a closed form and each established as a polynomial identity in the jets of
the fields, for a completely general four-dimensional metric. The reduced action follows by integrating over the
circle. @overduin1998 [Sec. 3.4] and @duff1994 [Sec. 2] quote the result; the derivation is ours.

### Jets

A formula for the curvature of the ansatz must hold for every four-dimensional metric, every vector and every
scalar. The way to verify such a formula once and for all is to note that curvature at a point depends only on
finitely many numbers, the values and derivatives of the fields there, and to treat these numbers as independent
variables.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-jet-variables}
#### Jet variables

The **jets** of the fields at a point are the values and first and second partial derivatives $g_{\mu\nu}$,
$\partial_\rho g_{\mu\nu}$, $\partial_\rho\partial_\sigma g_{\mu\nu}$, $A_\mu$, $\partial_\rho A_\mu$, $\partial_\rho\partial_\sigma A_\mu$, $\phi$,
$\partial_\rho\phi$, $\partial_\rho\partial_\sigma\phi$, together with symbols $g^{\mu\nu}$ for the inverse metric, treated as
independent real numbers. The curvature of a metric at a point is a polynomial in its jets and $g^{\mu\nu}$, with
$\partial_\rho g^{\mu\nu} = -g^{\mu\alpha}\partial_\rho g_{\alpha\beta}g^{\beta\nu}$ as the derivative of the inverse; an identity
between curvatures that holds for all values of the jets holds for all metrics.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Christoffel symbols are the first objects built from jets. The first example records their polynomial degree,
which bounds the size of the computation.

::: {#exm-jets-christoffel}
#### The Christoffel symbols as jets

$\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12g^{\lambda\kappa}(\partial_\mu g_{\kappa\nu} + \partial_\nu g_{\kappa\mu} - \partial_\kappa g_{\mu\nu})$ is a polynomial
of degree two in the jets, and $\partial_\rho\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$, by the product rule with the derivative of $g^{\lambda\kappa}$, of
degree three.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** This is how `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Jets` defines `Γ4` and `dΓ4`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The five-dimensional jets are not new variables. The second example expresses them through the four-dimensional
ones, which is where the cylinder condition enters.

::: {#exm-jets-ansatz}
#### The jets of the ansatz

The five-dimensional jets are polynomials in the four-dimensional ones: $\partial_\rho\hat g_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\rho g_{\mu\nu} -
2\phi\partial_\rho\phi A_\mu A_\nu - \phi^2(\partial_\rho A_\mu A_\nu + A_\mu\partial_\rho A_\nu)$ and so on, with every $y$-derivative zero
(@def-cylinder-condition). The symmetries $\partial_\rho\partial_\sigma = \partial_\sigma\partial_\rho$ and $g_{\mu\nu} = g_{\nu\mu}$ are
imposed by taking one variable for each unordered pair of indices.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** These symmetries are built into symmetrised accessors of the jet structure of `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Jets`.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The jet model raises a question about the inverse metric, whose symbols are independent of the metric jets. The third
example shows that the relation between them is never needed for the reduction formulas.

::: {#exm-jets-sage}
#### Derivations on the jet ring

The jets and the symbols $g^{\mu\nu}$ generate a polynomial ring, and $\partial_\rho$ acts on it as a derivation: it obeys the
product rule, sends the values to the first jets and the first jets to the second, and sends $g^{\mu\nu}$ to
$-g^{\mu\alpha}\partial_\rho g_{\alpha\beta}g^{\beta\nu}$. Every identity below holds in this ring with $g^{\mu\nu}$ as free symbols,
once $\phi^{-1}\phi = 1$ is used: the relation $g^{\mu\lambda}g_{\lambda\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nu$ is never needed, so the reduction formulas
are identities between polynomials (@prp-kk-scalar), unlike the Weyl formula of @exm-kkr-weyl-true-inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** The proofs in `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Jets` are plain `ring` identities, with $g^{\mu\nu}$ free.

**Sage.** The same jet model is implemented independently in `sage/kk_jets.sage`, which builds the polynomial ring of
the jets, differentiates with a derivation implementing the rule for $\partial_\rho g^{\mu\nu}$, and finds every identity
with $g^{\mu\nu}$ free.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The two new terms of the reduced curvature scalar, checked with SageManifolds on metrics with flat spacetime
part. Left: $A = 0$ and $\phi = \phi(x)$ gives $\hat R = 2\phi''/\phi = -\tfrac{2}{\phi}\Box\phi$ ($\Box\phi = -\phi''$ in
the signature $(+, -, -, -)$). Right: $\phi = 1$ and a constant electric field $F_{tx} = B$ gives $\hat R =
\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = -\tfrac12B^2$, the points being
SageManifolds values. Generated by
`figures/kk_dilaton_curvature.sage`.](figures/kk_dilaton_curvature.svg){#fig-kk-dilaton-curvature width=90%}

The first exercise counts the jets. The count shows why the computation is done by machine but also that it is
finite.

::: {#exr-kkr-jets-count}
#### How many jets?

Count the independent jets of $g_{\mu\nu}$, $A_\mu$ and $\phi$ up to second order in four dimensions, together with the
symbols $g^{\mu\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g_{\mu\nu}$ has $10$ values, $4 \times 10 = 40$ first derivatives and $10 \times 10 = 100$ second derivatives (symmetric
pairs $\rho\sigma$ times symmetric pairs $\mu\nu$); $A_\mu$ has $4 + 16 + 40 = 60$; $\phi$ has $1 + 4 + 10 = 15$; and $g^{\mu\nu}$
adds $10$. In all $150 + 60 + 15 + 10 = 235$ variables, and $\hat R$ is a polynomial in them (and $\phi^{-1}$) with a few
thousand terms (@exm-kkr-scalar-size).
:::

The rule for the derivative of the inverse metric is the only analytic input of the jet model. The second exercise
checks it with Sage on a matrix of arbitrary functions.

::: {#exr-kkr-jets-inverse-derivative}
#### The derivative of the inverse

Derive $\partial_\rho g^{\mu\nu} = -g^{\mu\alpha}\partial_\rho g_{\alpha\beta}g^{\beta\nu}$ by differentiating $g^{\mu\alpha}g_{\alpha\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nu$,
and verify it with Sage for a symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix of functions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_\rho(g^{\mu\alpha}g_{\alpha\nu}) = 0$ gives $(\partial_\rho g^{\mu\alpha})g_{\alpha\nu} = -g^{\mu\alpha}\partial_\rho g_{\alpha\nu}$; multiplying by
$g^{\nu\beta}$ gives the rule. In matrix form $\partial g^{-1} = -g^{-1}(\partial g)g^{-1}$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-jets-inverse-derivative >}}
:::

The jet model treats $g^{\mu\nu}$ as unrelated to $g_{\mu\nu}$. The third exercise asks why the resulting identities are
still statements about metrics.

::: {#exr-kkr-jets-free-inverse}
#### Free inverse symbols

Suppose an identity $P(j, \bar g) = 0$ holds for all values of the jets $j$ and of independent symbols $\bar g^{\mu\nu}$.
Explain why it holds for every metric, and why the converse fails: an identity can hold for metrics without holding
with free symbols.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For a metric, substitute its jets at a point for $j$ and its true inverse for $\bar g$; an identity valid for all values
remains valid for these. Conversely an identity may need $\bar g^{\mu\lambda}g_{\lambda\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nu$, which free symbols do
not satisfy; for instance $\bar g^{\mu\nu}g_{\mu\nu} = 4$ holds for every metric but not with free symbols. The reduction
formulas happen to hold in the stronger free form (@exm-jets-sage), which makes their proofs pure ring
normalisation; the Weyl formula of @prp-weyl-curvature does not, and needs the true inverse.
:::
::::

### The Christoffel symbols

The first step of the reduction is the Levi-Civita connection of the ansatz (@sec-levi-civita). Its symbols fall into
six groups according to how many indices point along the circle, and each group is a four-dimensional object built
from $g$, $F$ and $\phi$.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-christoffel-patterns}
#### Christoffel symbols of the ansatz

With $F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu$, indices raised with $g^{\mu\nu}$ and $\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$ the Levi-Civita
symbols of $g$, the five-dimensional symbols $\hat\Gamma^A_{BC}$ fall into six patterns:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} &= \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12\phi^2(A_\mu F_\nu{}^\lambda + A_\nu F_\mu{}^\lambda) + \phi A_\mu A_\nu\partial^\lambda\phi, &
\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu y} &= -\tfrac12\phi^2F_\mu{}^\lambda + \phi A_\mu\partial^\lambda\phi, &
\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy} &= \phi\,\partial^\lambda\phi, \\
\hat\Gamma^y_{\mu\nu} &= \tfrac{1}{\phi}(A_\mu\partial_\nu\phi + A_\nu\partial_\mu\phi) + \tfrac12(\partial_\mu A_\nu + \partial_\nu A_\mu) - A_\lambda\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}, &
\hat\Gamma^y_{\mu y} &= \tfrac{\partial_\mu\phi}{\phi} - A_\lambda\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu y}, &
\hat\Gamma^y_{yy} &= -A_\lambda\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-kk-christoffel}
(@prp-kk-christoffel). Each is a polynomial identity in the jets and $\phi^{-1}$. Every term depends on $\phi$ only
through $\phi^2$, so these are the formulas of the mostly-plus literature with $\phi^2 \to -\phi^2$; the three
symbols with an upper $y$ keep their form, written through the $\hat\Gamma^\lambda$, under the switch.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The symbols with an upper spacetime index enter the geodesic equation of a particle as seen in four dimensions. The
first example reads off the force exerted by a varying circle.

::: {#exm-christoffel-upper-spacetime}
#### The symbols with an upper spacetime index

$\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$ is the four-dimensional symbol plus terms in $A$ and $F$: for $A = 0$ it reduces to
$\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$ exactly, and $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy} = \phi\partial^\lambda\phi$ enters the geodesic equation as $\ddot x^\lambda = -\phi\,\partial^\lambda\phi\,\dot y^2$:
since $\partial^i\phi = -\partial_i\phi$ in this signature, a particle moving along the circle feels a force
$\phi\nabla\phi\,\dot y^2$ pushing it towards large circles, where its Kaluza-Klein mass $|n|/\phi$ is smallest
(@sec-kk-tower).
:::

The symbols with an upper $y$ have a common structure. The second example explains it through the mixed entries of
the inverse metric.

::: {#exm-christoffel-upper-y}
#### The symbols with an upper $y$

Each contains $-A_\lambda\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\cdots}$, the trace of the mixed inverse entries $\hat g^{y\lambda} = -A^\lambda$; the
$A$-independent parts are $\partial_\mu\phi/\phi$ and $\tfrac12(\partial_\mu A_\nu + \partial_\nu A_\mu)$, the symmetric part of $\partial A$ that
does not enter $F$.
:::

The contracted symbol $\hat\Gamma^A_{A\mu}$ is the derivative of the logarithm of the volume element. The third example
checks this standard identity against @eq-kk-volume.

::: {#exm-christoffel-trace}
#### The trace

$\hat\Gamma^A_{A\mu} = \Gamma^\lambda_{\lambda\mu} + \partial_\mu\phi/\phi = \partial_\mu\ln(\phi\sqrt{-g})$, in agreement with
$\partial_\mu\ln\sqrt{|\hat g|}$ and @eq-kk-volume; all the $A$-dependence cancels in the trace (@exr-kk-christoffel).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise compares the six patterns with SageManifolds on a five-dimensional metric with arbitrary functions.
It is an independent check of @prp-kk-christoffel on a large family of metrics.

::: {#exr-kk-christoffel}
#### The Christoffel symbols with SageManifolds

Compute the Levi-Civita symbols of the ansatz for a diagonal $g$ with arbitrary functions and compare with
@eq-kk-christoffel.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kk-christoffel >}}
:::

One pattern can be derived in two lines. The second exercise does so, as a model for the derivation of the others.

::: {#exr-kkr-christoffel-yy}
#### Deriving $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy}$

Derive $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy} = \phi\,\partial^\lambda\phi$ from $\hat\Gamma^A_{BC} = \tfrac12\hat g^{AD}(\partial_B\hat g_{DC} + \partial_C\hat g_{DB} -
\partial_D\hat g_{BC})$ and @eq-kk-inverse.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $B = C = y$ and the cylinder condition, $\partial_y\hat g_{Dy} = 0$, so $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy} = -\tfrac12\hat g^{\lambda D}\partial_D\hat
g_{yy} = -\tfrac12\hat g^{\lambda\mu}\partial_\mu(-\phi^2)$, the term with $D = y$ vanishing because $\partial_y\hat g_{yy} = 0$. With
$\hat g^{\lambda\mu} = g^{\lambda\mu}$ this is $g^{\lambda\mu}\phi\partial_\mu\phi = \phi\,\partial^\lambda\phi$. No $A$ appears because $\hat
g^{\lambda\mu}$ is $A$-independent.
:::

The trace identity of @exm-christoffel-trace can be checked from the patterns. The third exercise asks for this
consistency check. Only the sum of two patterns is needed.

::: {#exr-kkr-christoffel-trace}
#### The trace from the patterns

Compute $\hat\Gamma^A_{A\mu} = \hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\lambda\mu} + \hat\Gamma^y_{y\mu}$ from @eq-kk-christoffel and show that the $A$-dependent
terms cancel.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\lambda\mu} = \Gamma^\lambda_{\lambda\mu} - \tfrac12\phi^2(A_\lambda F_\mu{}^\lambda + A_\mu F_\lambda{}^\lambda) + \phi A_\lambda A_\mu\partial^\lambda\phi$, with
$F_\lambda{}^\lambda = 0$. And $\hat\Gamma^y_{y\mu} = \partial_\mu\phi/\phi - A_\lambda\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu y} = \partial_\mu\phi/\phi + \tfrac12\phi^2A_\lambda
F_\mu{}^\lambda - \phi A_\mu A_\lambda\partial^\lambda\phi$. The sum is $\Gamma^\lambda_{\lambda\mu} + \partial_\mu\phi/\phi$: the $AF$ and $AA\partial\phi$ terms
cancel pairwise, as they must since $\sqrt{|\hat g|} = \phi\sqrt{-g}$ does not depend on $A$.
:::
::::

### The Ricci tensor

The Ricci tensor (@sec-ricci) is the trace of the Riemann tensor and is what enters the vacuum Einstein equations. For
the ansatz it is most transparent in the frame of @exr-kkr-inverse-dual-frame, but the definition gives the
coordinate components, which are those stated below.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-ricci-components}
#### Ricci tensor of the ansatz

With $\Box\phi = g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\phi$ (for $g = \eta$, $\Box = \partial_t^2 - \nabla^2$) and $\nabla^\lambda F_{\lambda\mu}$ the
four-dimensional covariant divergence,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\hat R_{yy} &= \phi\,\Box\phi + \tfrac14\phi^4F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}, \\
\hat R_{\mu y} &= A_\mu\hat R_{yy} + \tfrac12\phi^2\nabla^\lambda F_{\lambda\mu} - \tfrac32\phi\,\partial_\lambda\phi\,F_\mu{}^\lambda, \\
\hat R_{\mu\nu} &= R_{\mu\nu} + \tfrac12\phi^2F_\mu{}^\lambda F_{\nu\lambda} - \tfrac{1}{\phi}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\phi
  + A_\mu\hat R_{\nu y} + A_\nu\hat R_{\mu y} - A_\mu A_\nu\hat R_{yy},
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-kk-ricci}
(@prp-kk-ricci). The combinations $\hat R_{\mu y} - A_\mu\hat R_{yy}$ and $\hat R_{\mu\nu} - A_\mu\hat R_{\nu y} - A_\nu\hat R_{\mu y} +
A_\mu A_\nu\hat R_{yy}$ are the components in the frame $(dx^\mu, dy + A)$, free of $A$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The circle-circle component involves only the scalar and the Maxwell invariant. The first example draws the
consequence for Kaluza's original choice $\phi = 1$.

::: {#exm-ricci-yy}
#### The $yy$ component

Only the scalar and the Maxwell invariant appear: the vacuum equation $\hat R_{yy} = 0$ is $\Box\phi = -\tfrac14\phi^3F^2$,
so a constant $\phi$ is consistent only when $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = 0$, Jordan and Thiry's observation that Kaluza's
$\phi = 1$ is inconsistent [@overduin1998, Sec. 3.4].
:::

The mixed component contains the divergence of the field strength. The second example identifies its vacuum
equation as Maxwell's equation.

::: {#exm-ricci-mixed}
#### The mixed component

$\hat R_{\mu y} - A_\mu\hat R_{yy} = \tfrac12\phi^2\nabla^\lambda F_{\lambda\mu} - \tfrac32\phi\partial_\lambda\phi F_\mu{}^\lambda$: the vacuum
equation $\hat R_{\mu y} = 0$ is Maxwell's equation $\nabla^\lambda F_{\lambda\mu} = 3\phi^{-1}\partial_\lambda\phi\,F_\mu{}^\lambda$ with the
scalar as a source [@overduin1998, eq. 6]; for constant $\phi$ it is $\nabla^\lambda F_{\lambda\mu} = 0$.
:::

The spacetime components complete the picture. The third example identifies the five-dimensional vacuum equations
with Einstein's equations coupled to the electromagnetic field.

::: {#exm-ricci-spacetime}
#### The spacetime components

$\hat R_{\mu\nu}$ contains the four-dimensional Ricci tensor, the Maxwell stress term $\tfrac12\phi^2F_\mu{}^\lambda F_{\nu\lambda}$ and
the scalar's second derivatives: the vacuum equation $\hat R_{\mu\nu} = 0$ is Einstein's equation with the
electromagnetic stress tensor of @exm-stress-maxwell and a scalar source.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the circle-circle component on two explicit metrics with SageManifolds. The two
configurations isolate the two terms of $\hat R_{yy}$.

::: {#exr-kkr-ricci-yy-check}
#### $\hat R_{yy}$ on examples

With SageManifolds, compute $\hat R_{yy}$ for $\eta - \phi(t, x)^2dy^2$ and for the constant electric field $A_x = Bt$
with $\phi = 1$, and compare with @eq-kk-ricci.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For the first metric $\Box\phi = \phi_{tt} - \phi_{xx}$, for the second $F^2 = -2B^2$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-ricci-yy-check >}}
:::

The frame components of the Ricci tensor are free of $A$. The second exercise derives them from the coordinate
components, which is how @eq-kk-ricci was organised.

::: {#exr-kkr-ricci-frame}
#### The frame components

With the frame $(h_\mu, \partial_y)$ of @exr-kkr-inverse-dual-frame, show that $\hat R(h_\mu, \partial_y) = \hat R_{\mu y} - A_\mu\hat
R_{yy}$ and $\hat R(h_\mu, h_\nu) = \hat R_{\mu\nu} - A_\mu\hat R_{\nu y} - A_\nu\hat R_{\mu y} + A_\mu A_\nu\hat R_{yy}$, and write these with
@eq-kk-ricci.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
By bilinearity, $\hat R(\partial_\mu - A_\mu\partial_y, \partial_y) = \hat R_{\mu y} - A_\mu\hat R_{yy}$ and $\hat R(h_\mu, h_\nu) = \hat R_{\mu\nu} -
A_\nu\hat R_{\mu y} - A_\mu\hat R_{y\nu} + A_\mu A_\nu\hat R_{yy}$. Inserting @eq-kk-ricci, the frame components are
$\tfrac12\phi^2\nabla^\lambda F_{\lambda\mu} - \tfrac32\phi\partial_\lambda\phi F_\mu{}^\lambda$ and $R_{\mu\nu} + \tfrac12\phi^2F_\mu{}^\lambda F_{\nu\lambda} -
\phi^{-1}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\phi$: tensors on spacetime built from $g$, $F$ and $\phi$, gauge invariant as they must be.
:::

Kaluza set $\phi = 1$. The third exercise writes the five-dimensional vacuum equations for constant $\phi$ and finds
the price.

::: {#exr-kkr-ricci-constant-phi}
#### Constant $\phi$

Write the vacuum equations $\hat R_{AB} = 0$ for $\phi = 1$ as four-dimensional equations. Which of them is a constraint
on the electromagnetic field?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In the frame: $\hat R_{yy} = \tfrac14F^2 = 0$, $\tfrac12\nabla^\lambda F_{\lambda\mu} = 0$ and $R_{\mu\nu} + \tfrac12F_\mu{}^\lambda F_{\nu\lambda} = 0$.
The second is Maxwell's equation and the third Einstein's equation with the electromagnetic stress tensor, while the
first, $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = 2(B^2 - E^2) = 0$, is an unphysical constraint: a static Coulomb field violates it. Keeping
$\phi$ dynamical removes the constraint, at the price of a scalar field (@exm-ricci-yy).
:::
::::

### The curvature scalar and the action

Contracting the Ricci tensor with the inverse metric gives the curvature scalar, the Lagrangian of the
Einstein-Hilbert action. The $A$-dependent terms of @eq-kk-ricci cancel in the contraction, and what remains is the
central formula of the theory.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-kk-curvature-scalar}
#### The reduced curvature scalar

$$
\hat R = R + \tfrac14\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} - \tfrac{2}{\phi}\Box\phi
$$ {#eq-kk-scalar}
(@prp-kk-scalar): the four-dimensional scalar, the Maxwell invariant with the coefficient $\tfrac14\phi^2$ (it becomes
the Maxwell Lagrangian $-\tfrac14F^2$ once the sign of the Einstein-Hilbert action in this signature is included,
@def-reduced-action), and a total derivative in disguise. It follows from @eq-kk-ricci by $\hat R = \hat g^{AB}\hat R_{AB}$ with @eq-kk-inverse, all
$A$-dependent terms cancelling.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
With the vector switched off and a flat spacetime metric, only the last term survives. The first example evaluates it
and connects it with the two-dimensional toy.

::: {#exm-scalar-dilaton}
#### Scalar only

$g = \eta$, $A = 0$, $\phi = \phi(x)$: $\Box\phi = -\phi''$ and $\hat R = 2\phi''/\phi$, the left panel of
@fig-kk-dilaton-curvature; the $(x, y)$ block $-dx^2 - \phi^2dy^2$ is the negative of the two-dimensional toy of
@exr-kk-toy, whose curvature $-2\phi''/\phi$ changes sign under $g \to -g$ (@exr-kk-dilaton).
:::

With $\phi = 1$ and a flat spacetime metric, only the Maxwell term survives. The second example evaluates it for a
constant electric field.

::: {#exm-scalar-electric}
#### Electric field only

$g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$, $A_x = Bt$: $F_{tx} = B$, $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = -2B^2$ and $\hat R = -\tfrac12B^2$, the right panel of
@fig-kk-dilaton-curvature: a flat four-dimensional metric with a constant electromagnetic field is a curved
five-dimensional space.
:::

With both switched off, the reduction is trivial. The third example records it, since it identifies the vacuum
solutions. It is the background of all perturbative statements.

::: {#exm-scalar-flat}
#### The flat limit

$A = 0$, $\phi$ constant: $\hat R = R$; the five-dimensional vacuum equations reduce to the four-dimensional ones,
and $M_4 \times S^1$ with $M_4$ Ricci flat is a solution (@exm-ansatz-ground-state).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the scalar term on the configuration of @exm-scalar-dilaton and shows that its contribution
to the action is a total derivative. It is the computation behind the left panel of @fig-kk-dilaton-curvature.

::: {#exr-kk-dilaton}
#### The dilaton term is a total derivative

For $\eta - \phi(x)^2dy^2$, compute $\hat R$ and show that $\sqrt{|\hat g|}\,\hat R$ is a total derivative.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kk-dilaton >}}
:::

A magnetic field has the opposite sign of $F^2$ to an electric one. The second exercise checks that the curvature
follows the sign.

::: {#exr-kkr-scalar-magnetic}
#### A constant magnetic field

With SageManifolds, compute $\hat R$ for $g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$ and $A_z = Bx$. Compare the sign with
@exm-scalar-electric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_{xz} = B$ and $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} = 2F_{xz}F^{xz} = 2B^2\eta^{xx}\eta^{zz} = 2B^2$, so $\hat R = \tfrac14F^2 = \tfrac12B^2$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-scalar-magnetic >}}

In general $F^2 = 2(B^2 - E^2)$, so electric and magnetic fields curve the five-dimensional space with opposite signs.
:::

Much of the literature uses the signature $(-, +, +, +, +)$. The third exercise translates @eq-kk-scalar, which is a
useful check of every sign in it.

::: {#exr-kkr-scalar-mostly-plus}
#### The mostly-plus form

Under $\hat g \to -\hat g$ (so $g \to -g$, $\phi^2 \to -\phi^2$ in the parametrisation), how do $\hat R$, $R$,
$F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ and $\Box$ change? Derive the mostly-plus form of @eq-kk-scalar for $d\hat s^2 = g + \phi^2(dy +
A)^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Christoffel symbols and the Ricci tensor are unchanged by $\hat g \to -\hat g$, while one inverse metric changes sign:
$\hat R \to -\hat R$, $R \to -R$, $\Box \to -\Box$, and $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$, with two inverse metrics, is unchanged. The
mostly-plus metric $g_+ + \phi^2(dy + A)^2$ is $-(g - \phi^2(dy + A)^2)$ with $g = -g_+$, so $-\hat R_+ = -R_+ + \tfrac14\phi^2F^2 +
\tfrac{2}{\phi}\Box_+\phi$, that is $\hat R_+ = R_+ - \tfrac14\phi^2F^2 - \tfrac{2}{\phi}\Box_+\phi$, the form usually quoted in the
mostly-plus literature.
:::
::::

The five-dimensional action is the integral of the curvature scalar against the volume element. With @eq-kk-volume and
@eq-kk-scalar the circle integral is trivial, and the result is a four-dimensional action.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-reduced-action}
#### The reduced action

Inserting @eq-kk-scalar and @eq-kk-volume into the five-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert action and integrating over
the circle of circumference $2\pi$,
$$
\hat S = -\frac{1}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int d^5x\sqrt{|\hat g|}\,\hat R
  = -\frac{2\pi}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g}\,\phi\left(R + \tfrac14\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}\right) ,
$$ {#eq-kk-reduced-action}
the overall sign being that of the Einstein-Hilbert action in the signature $(+, -, -, -)$ (@eq-einstein-hilbert)
and the term $-2\sqrt{-g}\,\Box\phi = -2\partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}\,g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu\phi)$ being a total derivative
(@exr-kk-total-derivative). This is the **Jordan-frame** action [@overduin1998, eq. 9], with the Newton constant
$\kappa^2 = \hat\kappa^2/2\pi$ when $\phi = 1$ and the Maxwell term $-\tfrac14\phi^3F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ carrying the
factor $\phi^3$ and the standard sign.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

**Lean.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Kaluza's choice $\phi = 1$ gives the action he found. The first example writes it, with the caveat that the choice is
not consistent with the field equations.

::: {#exm-action-einstein-maxwell}
#### $\phi = 1$

$\hat S = -\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,(R + \tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}) = \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,(-R -
\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})$: Einstein gravity coupled to Maxwell's
electromagnetism with the gauge field in gravitational units, "the central miracle of Kaluza-Klein theory"
[@overduin1998, p. 15], but with the caveat of @exm-ricci-yy.
:::

Without the vector the action is a scalar-tensor theory. The second example identifies it and the observational
problem it poses.

::: {#exm-action-brans-dicke}
#### $A = 0$

$\hat S = -\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,\phi R$, the Brans-Dicke action with $\omega = 0$; observation requires $\omega >
500$, so the scalar must be frozen or made massive for a realistic theory [@overduin1998, Sec. 3.5]. The Weyl
rescaling of @sec-kk-einstein-frame shows it is a canonical massless scalar.
:::

The power of $\phi$ in front of $F^2$ has a physical meaning. The third example anticipates the Einstein frame, where it
becomes an exponential coupling of the dilaton.

::: {#exm-action-dilaton-coupling}
#### The dilaton coupling

The factor $\phi^3$ in front of $F^2$ means that the effective electric charge depends on the size of the circle:
in the Einstein frame it becomes $e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2$ with a canonical dilaton $\sigma$, the coupling $a = \sqrt3$ of
the Kaluza-Klein black holes [@duff1994, p. 30].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise justifies dropping the $\Box\phi$ term. It is the divergence identity for the d'Alembertian. The same identity is used again for the boundary term of the Einstein frame.

::: {#exr-kk-total-derivative}
#### Dropping $\Box\phi$

Show that $\sqrt{-g}\,\Box\phi = \partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}\,g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu\phi)$ and hence that the last term of
@eq-kk-scalar does not contribute to the action.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Box\phi = g^{\mu\nu}(\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi - \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\partial_\lambda\phi)$ and $g^{\mu\nu}\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{-g}}
\partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}g^{\mu\lambda})$ (@exm-christoffel-trace and the contracted Christoffel identity), so $\sqrt{-g}\Box\phi =
\sqrt{-g}g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi + \partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}g^{\mu\lambda})\partial_\lambda\phi = \partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g}g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu\phi)$.
Multiplied by the constant $-2\pi/2\hat\kappa^2$, this integrates to a boundary term, which vanishes for fields that
decay at infinity; note that the factor $\phi$ of @eq-kk-volume multiplies $-\tfrac{2}{\phi}\Box\phi$ to give exactly
$-2\Box\phi$, which is why no $(\partial\phi)^2$ term survives in @eq-kk-reduced-action.
:::

The Maxwell term of @eq-kk-reduced-action is not yet canonically normalised. The second exercise rescales the gauge
field, the step that introduces the gauge coupling of @sec-kk-tower.

::: {#exr-kkr-action-normalisation}
#### Canonical normalisation

For $\phi = 1$, write $A_\mu = \sqrt2\kappa\,\mathcal{A}_\mu$ and show that the Maxwell part of @eq-kk-reduced-action becomes
the canonical $-\tfrac14\int\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal{F}_{\mu\nu}\mathcal{F}^{\mu\nu}$. Where does the gauge coupling appear once the
field is canonical?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Maxwell part is $-\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\cdot\tfrac14\int\sqrt{-g}F^2$, and $F = \sqrt2\kappa\,\mathcal{F}$ gives $F^2 =
2\kappa^2\mathcal{F}^2$, so it is $-\tfrac14\int\sqrt{-g}\,\mathcal{F}^2$. The coupling then sits in the covariant
derivatives of charged fields: a field that couples to $A$ through $\partial_\mu - iqA_\mu$ couples to $\mathcal{A}$ through
$\partial_\mu - iq\sqrt2\kappa\,\mathcal{A}_\mu$, so its charge in canonical units is $\sqrt2\kappa q$. With $q = n/R$ for the
Kaluza-Klein modes this is the charge $ne$ with $e = \sqrt2\kappa/R$ of @def-charge-quantisation: gravitational strength
divided by the radius.
:::

The scalar has its own field equation. The third exercise derives it from the reduced action and checks it against the
five-dimensional equations.

::: {#exr-kkr-action-dilaton-equation}
#### The equation of the scalar

Vary @eq-kk-reduced-action with respect to $\phi$ and show that $R + \tfrac34\phi^2F^2 = 0$. Show that the same equation
follows from $\hat R = 0$ and $\hat R_{yy} = 0$ with @eq-kk-scalar and @eq-kk-ricci.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Lagrangian is $\sqrt{-g}(\phi R + \tfrac14\phi^3F^2)$ up to a constant, with no derivatives of $\phi$, so the
Euler-Lagrange equation is $\partial/\partial\phi = 0$: $R + \tfrac34\phi^2F^2 = 0$. In five dimensions $\hat R_{AB} = 0$
implies $\hat R = 0$, that is $R + \tfrac14\phi^2F^2 - 2\phi^{-1}\Box\phi = 0$, and $\hat R_{yy} = 0$ gives $\Box\phi = -
\tfrac14\phi^3F^2$; substituting, $R + \tfrac14\phi^2F^2 + \tfrac12\phi^2F^2 = R + \tfrac34\phi^2F^2 = 0$. The two
descriptions agree, as they must for a consistent truncation.
:::
::::

The three propositions of this section state the three closed formulas as identities in the jets. The first
concerns the Christoffel symbols and holds pattern by pattern.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kk-christoffel}
#### The Christoffel symbols

The six patterns @eq-kk-christoffel hold as polynomial identities in the jets with $g^{\mu\nu}$ free, for $\phi \neq 0$.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The patterns are easy to test on a constant electromagnetic field, where all derivatives of $g$ and $\phi$ vanish. The
first example quotes the result of @exr-kkr-christoffel-electric.

::: {#exm-kkr-christoffel-electric}
#### A constant electric field

For $g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$ and $A_x = Bt$, @eq-kk-christoffel gives $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu y} = -\tfrac12F_\mu{}^\lambda$, so
$\hat\Gamma^t_{xy} = -\tfrac12F_x{}^t = -\tfrac12F_{xt}\eta^{tt} = \tfrac12B$ and $\hat\Gamma^x_{ty} = -\tfrac12F_{tx}\eta^{xx} =
\tfrac12B$, as @exr-kkr-christoffel-electric finds; $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy} = 0$ because $\phi$ is constant.
:::

A curvature formula can be established as an identity in the jets or computed on explicit metrics. The second example
compares the two routes, each of which detects errors the other misses.

::: {#exm-kkr-christoffel-coverage}
#### Jets and explicit metrics

An identity between polynomials in the jets holds for every metric at every point. A computation on explicit metrics,
such as a diagonal $g$ with arbitrary functions and generic $A$ and $\phi$ (@exr-kk-christoffel), uses the true inverse
metric but covers only an infinite yet special family. A sign error in a term with an off-diagonal component of $g$
would escape the second computation but not the first.
:::

**Lean.** The jet identities are `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Jets.Γ5_lll`, `Γ5_lly`, `Γ5_lyy`, `Γ5_yll`, `Γ5_yly`,
`Γ5_yyy`.

**Sage.** The explicit family is the SageManifolds computation of @exr-kk-christoffel.
:::

Each pattern is one identity for all index values at once. The third example spells out what one such identity says
and how it is proved.

::: {#exm-kkr-christoffel-lean-shape}
#### One pattern for all indices

The pattern for $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu y}$ states that for every value of the jets and all $\mu$, $\lambda$, the Christoffel symbol
$\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu y}$ computed from the five-dimensional jets of @exm-jets-ansatz equals the right-hand side of the
corresponding line of @eq-kk-christoffel. The proof expands both sides as polynomials in the jets, after clearing the
powers of $\phi^{-1}$ in the patterns that contain them, and uses no relation between $g^{\mu\nu}$ and $g_{\mu\nu}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Jets.Γ5_lly` states that for every jet configuration and all $\mu$, $\lambda$ the symbol
`Γ5 (inl λ) (inl μ) (inr ())` equals the right-hand side of the pattern. The proof unfolds the definitions with
`simp only` and closes the goal with `ring`, preceded by `field_simp` for the patterns that contain $\phi^{-1}$, without
any lemma about the inverse metric.

**Sage.** Pending.
