::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise carries out the electric-field check of @exm-kkr-christoffel-electric for all six patterns. It is
done with SageManifolds. All terms with derivatives of the metric or the scalar drop out.

::: {#exr-kkr-christoffel-electric}
#### The patterns for a constant field

Compute all Christoffel symbols of the ansatz with $g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$, $A_x = Bt$ and compare with the patterns.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\Gamma = 0$ and $\partial\phi = 0$ the patterns reduce to $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu y} = -\tfrac12F_\mu{}^\lambda$, $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}
= -\tfrac12(A_\mu F_\nu{}^\lambda + A_\nu F_\mu{}^\lambda)$, $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy} = 0$ and $\hat\Gamma^y_{\mu y} = -A_\lambda\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu y}$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-christoffel-electric >}}
:::

The geodesics of the ansatz describe charged particles. The second exercise derives the Lorentz force from the
patterns, Kaluza's second miracle.

::: {#exr-kkr-christoffel-lorentz}
#### The Lorentz force

For $\phi = 1$, show that $p_y = \hat g_{yA}\dot x^A = -(\dot y + A_\mu\dot x^\mu)$ is constant along a geodesic, and that the
spacetime components of the geodesic equation become $\ddot x^\lambda + \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu = p_y\,F^\lambda{}_\mu\dot x^\mu$
(dots are derivatives with respect to the five-dimensional proper parameter).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_y$ is Killing, so $\hat g(\partial_y, \dot x) = p_y$ is conserved along geodesics. With $\phi = 1$ the patterns give
$\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy} = 0$, $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu y} = -\tfrac12F_\mu{}^\lambda$ and $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} = \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} -
\tfrac12(A_\mu F_\nu{}^\lambda + A_\nu F_\mu{}^\lambda)$, so $\ddot x^\lambda + \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu - A_\mu\dot x^\mu F_\nu{}^\lambda\dot x^\nu -
F_\mu{}^\lambda\dot x^\mu\dot y = 0$, that is $\ddot x^\lambda + \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu = F_\mu{}^\lambda\dot x^\mu(\dot y + A_\nu\dot
x^\nu) = -p_yF_\mu{}^\lambda\dot x^\mu = p_yF^\lambda{}_\mu\dot x^\mu$. This is the Lorentz force with charge-to-mass ratio proportional to
$p_y$: the charge is the momentum around the circle (@exm-isometry-charge).
:::

The patterns must be symmetric in their two lower indices, since the connection is torsion free. The third exercise
checks the only non-obvious case.

::: {#exr-kkr-christoffel-symmetric}
#### Symmetry in the lower indices

Check that the expressions for $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$ and $\hat\Gamma^y_{\mu\nu}$ in @eq-kk-christoffel are symmetric in $\mu\nu$,
and explain why $\hat\Gamma^A_{\mu y} = \hat\Gamma^A_{y\mu}$ needs no check.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$ is symmetric, the bracket $A_\mu F_\nu{}^\lambda + A_\nu F_\mu{}^\lambda$ and $A_\mu A_\nu$ are symmetric by
construction, and so are $A_\mu\partial_\nu\phi + A_\nu\partial_\mu\phi$ and $\partial_\mu A_\nu + \partial_\nu A_\mu$; $-A_\lambda\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$
inherits the symmetry. The patterns with a lower $y$ define $\hat\Gamma^A_{\mu y}$, and $\hat\Gamma^A_{y\mu}$ is the same number
because the Levi-Civita connection is torsion free: the pattern list has six entries rather than eight for this
reason.
:::
::::

The second proposition concerns the Ricci tensor. Its proof is the longest of the three, since the Ricci tensor
contains derivatives of the Christoffel symbols.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-kk-ricci}
#### The Ricci tensor

The three formulas @eq-kk-ricci hold as polynomial identities in the jets.
:::

the number of monomials in each component.

::: {#exm-kkr-ricci-sizes}
#### How large are the identities?

Expanded in the jets, $\hat R_{00}$ has $1403$ monomials, $\hat R_{04}$ has $933$ and $\hat R_{44}$ has $418$
(index $4$ being $y$); the right-hand sides of @eq-kk-ricci, written through $\nabla$ and $F$, are a few lines, and
expanded in the jets they are the same polynomials.
:::

The constant electric field gives explicit values. The second example quotes them from @exr-kkr-ricci-electric. They show how the coordinate components depend on the gauge.

::: {#exm-kkr-ricci-electric-values}
#### The electric field again

For $g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$, $A_x = Bt$: $\hat R_{tt} = -\tfrac12B^2$, $\hat R_{xx} = \tfrac12B^2 - \tfrac12B^4t^2$ and $\hat
R_{xy} = -\tfrac12B^3t$. The $t$-dependence is only in the coordinate components: in the frame of @exr-kkr-ricci-frame
the components are $\tfrac12F_\mu{}^\lambda F_{\nu\lambda}$ and $\tfrac14F^2 = -\tfrac12B^2$, constants.
:::

The proposition turns the five-dimensional vacuum equations into four-dimensional ones. The third example lists the
resulting system. It is the form in which the proposition is used in the integrative exercises.

::: {#exm-kkr-ricci-vacuum}
#### The vacuum equations

$\hat R_{AB} = 0$ is equivalent, by @eq-kk-ricci, to the three four-dimensional equations $\phi\Box\phi = -\tfrac14\phi^4F^2$,
$\nabla^\lambda F_{\lambda\mu} = 3\phi^{-1}\partial_\lambda\phi F_\mu{}^\lambda$ and $R_{\mu\nu} = -\tfrac12\phi^2F_\mu{}^\lambda F_{\nu\lambda} +
\phi^{-1}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\phi$: Einstein-Maxwell theory with a scalar, every solution of which lifts to a Ricci-flat
five-dimensional metric (@exr-kkr-int-black-string).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks every component of the Ricci tensor on the constant electric field. It is the computation
behind @exm-kkr-ricci-electric-values.

::: {#exr-kkr-ricci-electric}
#### All components for a constant field

With SageManifolds, compute $\hat R_{AB}$ for $g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$, $A_x = Bt$ and compare with @eq-kk-ricci.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Here $\nabla^\lambda F_{\lambda\mu} = 0$ and $\partial\phi = 0$, so $\hat R_{yy} = \tfrac14F^2$, $\hat R_{\mu y} = A_\mu\hat R_{yy}$ and $\hat
R_{\mu\nu} = \tfrac12F_\mu{}^\lambda F_{\nu\lambda} + A_\mu\hat R_{\nu y} + A_\nu\hat R_{\mu y} - A_\mu A_\nu\hat R_{yy}$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-ricci-electric >}}
:::

The scalar terms of @eq-kk-ricci can be isolated by setting $A = 0$. The second exercise does so for a scalar
depending on two coordinates.

::: {#exr-kkr-ricci-dilaton-components}
#### The scalar terms

For $\eta - \phi(t, x)^2dy^2$, verify with SageManifolds that $\hat R_{\mu y} = 0$ and $\hat R_{\mu\nu} = -\phi^{-1}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $A = 0$, $g = \eta$ the formulas reduce to $\hat R_{\mu y} = 0$ and $\hat R_{\mu\nu} = -\phi^{-1}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\phi = -
\phi^{-1}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\phi$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-ricci-dilaton-components >}}
:::

The curvature scalar is the trace of the Ricci tensor. The third exercise performs the trace by hand in the frame,
which is the quickest route from @eq-kk-ricci to @eq-kk-scalar.

::: {#exr-kkr-ricci-trace}
#### From Ricci to the scalar

Using $\hat g^{AB} = \operatorname{diag}(g^{\mu\nu}, -\phi^{-2})$ in the frame $(h_\mu, \partial_y)$ and the frame components of
@exr-kkr-ricci-frame, derive @eq-kk-scalar.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\hat R = g^{\mu\nu}\hat R(h_\mu, h_\nu) - \phi^{-2}\hat R_{yy} = g^{\mu\nu}(R_{\mu\nu} + \tfrac12\phi^2F_\mu{}^\lambda F_{\nu\lambda} -
\phi^{-1}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\phi) - \phi^{-2}(\phi\Box\phi + \tfrac14\phi^4F^2)$. With $g^{\mu\nu}F_\mu{}^\lambda F_{\nu\lambda} = F^{\nu\lambda}F_{\nu\lambda} =
F^2$ this is $R + \tfrac12\phi^2F^2 - \phi^{-1}\Box\phi - \phi^{-1}\Box\phi - \tfrac14\phi^2F^2 = R + \tfrac14\phi^2F^2 -
\tfrac{2}{\phi}\Box\phi$.
:::
::::

The jet identity can also be tested on actual metrics. The second example does so with explicit polynomial fields, using no jets and no free inverse symbols.

#### An explicit configuration

Take all fifteen fields to be explicit polynomials in the four coordinates, build the five-dimensional metric, and
compute its curvature scalar as an exact rational function: it agrees with $R + \tfrac14\phi^2F^2 - \tfrac2\phi\Box\phi$
computed from the four-dimensional fields, and at a sample point all three terms are non-zero rational numbers, so

An electromagnetic plane wave has $F^2 = 0$ and lifts to a solution with $\phi = 1$. The third example uses
@prp-kk-scalar to see this.

::: {#exm-kkr-scalar-plane-wave}
#### A plane wave

For $g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$ and $A_x = f(t - z)$, $F_{tx} = f'$ and $F_{zx} = -f'$, so $F^2 = 2(-f'^2 + f'^2) = 0$ and $\hat
R = 0$: the plane wave satisfies the constraint of @exm-ricci-yy, and Kaluza's $\phi = 1$ is consistent for it. The
five-dimensional metric is a pp-wave, curved although $\hat R = 0$ (@exr-kkr-scalar-plane-wave).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise switches on both new terms of @eq-kk-scalar at once. It is a check that the two do not interfere.

::: {#exr-kkr-scalar-combined}
#### Both terms together

With SageManifolds, compute $\hat R$ for $g = \eta$, $A_z = Bv$ (with $v$ the third spatial coordinate) and $\phi = \phi(x)$,
and compare with @eq-kk-scalar.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_{vz} = B$, $F^2 = 2B^2$ and $\Box\phi = -\phi''$, so @eq-kk-scalar predicts $\hat R = \tfrac12\phi^2B^2 + 2\phi''/\phi$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-scalar-combined >}}
:::

The plane wave of @exm-kkr-scalar-plane-wave has vanishing curvature scalar but is not flat. The second exercise
computes its Ricci tensor.

::: {#exr-kkr-scalar-plane-wave}
#### The plane wave

Verify with SageManifolds that the ansatz with $g = \eta$, $\phi = 1$, $A_x = f(t - z)$ has $\hat R = 0$ and $\hat R_{yy} = 0$, and
compute $\hat R_{tt}$. Interpret the result with @exm-ricci-spacetime.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kkr-scalar-plane-wave >}}

$\hat R_{tt} = \tfrac12F_t{}^\lambda F_{t\lambda} = -\tfrac12f'^2$ is the Maxwell stress term of @exm-ricci-spacetime: the wave
carries energy, which curves the five-dimensional space, although the trace $F^2$ vanishes. The metric is not a
vacuum solution unless the four-dimensional metric responds to that energy.
:::

A constant circle of radius $R$ rescales the Maxwell term. The third exercise shows how the rescaling is absorbed,
which is why one may set $\phi = 1$ in the ground state without loss.

::: {#exr-kkr-scalar-constant-radius}
#### A constant radius

For constant $\phi = R$, show that @eq-kk-reduced-action is the $\phi = 1$ action with $A$ replaced by $RA$ and
$\hat\kappa^2$ by $\hat\kappa^2/R$. Which combination is the four-dimensional Newton constant?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\phi = R$: $-\frac{2\pi R}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}(R_4 + \tfrac14R^2F^2)$, and $R^2F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ is the Maxwell
invariant of $RA$. So the action is the $\phi = 1$ action for $(g, RA)$ with $2\pi/2\hat\kappa^2$ replaced by $2\pi
R/2\hat\kappa^2$, and the Newton constant is $\kappa^2 = \hat\kappa^2/2\pi R$, the five-dimensional one divided by the
circumference (@exr-frame-newton). The rescaled field $RA$ is the gauge field of the coordinate $Ry$, of period $2\pi
R$ (@exr-kkr-volume-circle).
:::
::::

## The Einstein frame {#sec-kk-einstein-frame}

The reduced action of @sec-kk-reduction multiplies the curvature scalar by the scalar field, so the strength of
gravity varies with the size of the circle. A rescaling of the four-dimensional metric by a power of $\phi$, a
Weyl rescaling, moves that factor into a kinetic term for the scalar and leaves the Einstein-Hilbert action in its
standard form. This section defines Weyl rescalings and their effect on curvature, the Jordan and Einstein frames,
and the dilaton, following @overduin1998 [Sec. 3.6] and @duff1994 [Sec. 2].

### Weyl rescalings

Two metrics that differ by a positive factor at each point have the same light cones and measure the same angles,
but they assign different lengths and different curvatures. Rescaling is the tool that trades a field-dependent
factor in front of the curvature for derivative terms of that factor.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-weyl-rescaling}
#### Weyl rescaling

A **Weyl rescaling** (conformal rescaling) of a metric is $\tilde g_{\mu\nu} = \Omega(x)^2g_{\mu\nu}$ with a positive
function $\Omega$: angles are preserved and lengths multiplied by $\Omega$. The inverse rescales by $\Omega^{-2}$ and the
volume element by $\Omega^n$ in $n$ dimensions, $\sqrt{-\tilde g} = \Omega^n\sqrt{-g}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
A rescaled sphere can be drawn as a surface whose profile follows $\Omega$. The first example is the one shown in
@fig-kk-einstein-frame.

::: {#exm-weyl-sphere}
#### Rescaling the sphere

$\tilde g = \Omega(\theta)^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$ with $\Omega = 1 + \tfrac12\cos\theta$: the left panel of
@fig-kk-einstein-frame shows the profile, stretched near the north pole and shrunk near the south; the curvature
is no longer constant (right panel).
:::

Many important metrics are rescalings of flat space. The second example lists two, one of which is used to test the
curvature formula below.

::: {#exm-weyl-flat}
#### Conformally flat metrics

$\tilde g = \Omega^2\eta$: every two-dimensional metric is locally of this form, and de Sitter space in conformal
time is $\Omega^2 = 1/(H\eta)^2$ times Minkowski space; the rescaling of @exm-weyl-four-dimensions is the
$\Omega = \Omega(t)$ case on the flat-slicing form.
:::

Fields respond to a rescaling according to how many inverse metrics their action contains. The third example
compares the Maxwell field with a scalar.

::: {#exm-weyl-matter}
#### Minimally coupled fields

The Maxwell action $\int\sqrt{-g}\,g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma}F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}$ is invariant under Weyl rescalings in four
dimensions ($\Omega^4\Omega^{-4} = 1$), while a massless scalar's action $\int\sqrt{-g}g^{\mu\nu}\partial\phi\partial\phi$ picks up
$\Omega^2$: this is why the Maxwell term of @eq-kk-reduced-action keeps only the $\phi^3$ from the Jordan frame
(@exr-kk-weyl).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the transformation of the inverse metric and of the volume element. These are the two
facts used in every later computation.

::: {#exr-kkr-weyl-volume}
#### Inverse and volume

Show that $\tilde g^{\mu\nu} = \Omega^{-2}g^{\mu\nu}$ and $\sqrt{|\tilde g|} = \Omega^n\sqrt{|g|}$ in $n$ dimensions, and compute how
$\sqrt{-g}\,R$ would scale under a constant rescaling in four dimensions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Omega^{-2}g^{\mu\lambda}\cdot\Omega^2g_{\lambda\nu} = \delta^\mu_\nu$, and $\det(\Omega^2g) = \Omega^{2n}\det g$ because each of the $n$ rows
is multiplied by $\Omega^2$. For constant $\Omega$ the Christoffel symbols and the Ricci tensor are unchanged and $\tilde R =
\Omega^{-2}R$, so $\sqrt{-\tilde g}\tilde R = \Omega^4\Omega^{-2}\sqrt{-g}R = \Omega^2\sqrt{-g}R$: the Einstein-Hilbert action is not
scale invariant in four dimensions, and a constant rescaling changes the effective Newton constant by $\Omega^{-2}$.
:::

The name "conformal" refers to the preservation of angles. The second exercise makes this precise and adds the
light cones.

::: {#exr-kkr-weyl-null-cones}
#### Angles and light cones

Show that a Weyl rescaling preserves the angle between two spacelike vectors and the set of null vectors. Is a
geodesic of $g$ a geodesic of $\tilde g$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tilde g(u, v)/\sqrt{\tilde g(u, u)\tilde g(v, v)} = \Omega^2g(u, v)/(\Omega^2\sqrt{g(u, u)g(v, v)})$, the same cosine, and $\tilde g(v, v) =
\Omega^2g(v, v)$ vanishes exactly when $g(v, v)$ does. Geodesics are not preserved in general: the Christoffel symbols
change by $\delta^\lambda_\mu\partial_\nu\ln\Omega + \delta^\lambda_\nu\partial_\mu\ln\Omega - g_{\mu\nu}\partial^\lambda\ln\Omega$. Null geodesics are
preserved as curves (with a different affine parameter), timelike ones are not: this is why "which frame do particles
follow" is a real question (@exm-jordan-geodesics).
:::

The Maxwell term is special in four dimensions. The third exercise finds the power of $\Omega$ it picks up in other
dimensions, with Sage.

::: {#exr-kkr-weyl-maxwell}
#### The Maxwell term in $n$ dimensions

Show that $\sqrt{|g|}\,g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma}F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}$ picks up $\Omega^{n - 4}$ under $g \to \Omega^2g$, and check with Sage for
$n = 2, \dots, 5$ with a generic metric and field strength.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\Omega^n$ from the volume element and $\Omega^{-4}$ from the two inverse metrics:

{{< sage exr-kkr-weyl-maxwell >}}

Classical electromagnetism is conformally invariant only in four dimensions.
:::
::::

The curvature of a rescaled metric involves derivatives of $\Omega$. The formula is classical, and it is what turns
the factor $\phi$ in front of $R$ into a kinetic term.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-weyl-curvature-formula}
#### Curvature under a Weyl rescaling

In four dimensions, for $\tilde g = \Omega^2g$,
$$
\tilde R = \Omega^{-2}\left(R - 6\,\Omega^{-1}\Box\Omega\right)
  = \Omega^{-2}\left(R - 6\,\Box\ln\Omega - 6\,g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\Omega\,\partial_\nu\ln\Omega\right),
$$ {#eq-weyl-curvature}
with $\Box = g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu$ the d'Alembertian of $g$ [@overduin1998, eq. 15], a formula valid in every
signature since $R$ and $\Box$ change sign together under $g \to -g$; in $n$ dimensions the coefficients are $2(n - 1)$ and
$(n - 1)(n - 2)$ (@prp-weyl-curvature).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In two dimensions the formula simplifies. The first example checks it on the rescaled sphere of @exm-weyl-sphere. It is also the content of the right panel of the figure below.

::: {#exm-weyl-two-dimensions}
#### Two dimensions

$\tilde R = \Omega^{-2}(R - 2\Box\ln\Omega)$: for the rescaled sphere of @exm-weyl-sphere SageManifolds gives exactly
this, with $R = 2$ (@fig-kk-einstein-frame). The absence of a $(\partial\ln\Omega)^2$ term is special to $n = 2$.
:::

The four-dimensional formula is tested on a time-dependent rescaling of de Sitter space. The second example records
the result of the direct computation.

::: {#exm-weyl-four-dimensions}
#### De Sitter with $\Omega(t)$

For $g$ de Sitter in flat slicing and $\Omega = \Omega(t)$, computing $\tilde R$ directly gives $\Omega^{-2}R - 6\Omega^{-3}
\Box\Omega$ exactly, and @exr-kk-weyl does the same for a static spherically symmetric metric with $\Omega(r)$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation with SageManifolds in `figures/kk_einstein_frame.sage`.
:::

A constant rescaling is the case without derivative terms. The third example isolates the first term of the formula. Dimensional analysis alone predicts it.

::: {#exm-weyl-constant}
#### Constant $\Omega$

$\tilde R = \Omega^{-2}R$: curvature has dimension of inverse length squared, and a constant rescaling of lengths by
$\Omega$ divides it by $\Omega^2$, the first term of @eq-weyl-curvature; all the rest comes from the derivatives of
$\Omega$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![Weyl rescaling. Left: the unit sphere (dashed) and the profile of the rescaled metric $\Omega^2g$ with $\Omega = 1 +
\tfrac12\cos\theta$. Right: the curvature scalar $R = 2$ of the sphere and $\tilde R = \Omega^{-2}(R - 2\Box\ln\Omega)$
of the rescaled metric, computed with SageManifolds; the four-dimensional formula is checked on de Sitter space in
the same script. Generated by
`figures/kk_einstein_frame.sage`.](figures/kk_einstein_frame.svg){#fig-kk-einstein-frame width=90%}

The two forms of @eq-weyl-curvature are equivalent. The first exercise proves this, which is a small computation with
the chain rule.

::: {#exr-kkr-weyl-log-form}
#### The logarithmic form

Show that $\Omega^{-1}\Box\Omega = \Box\ln\Omega + g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\Omega\,\partial_\nu\ln\Omega$, and hence that the two expressions in
@eq-weyl-curvature agree.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_\nu\ln\Omega = \Omega^{-1}\partial_\nu\Omega$, so $\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\ln\Omega = \Omega^{-1}\nabla_\mu\partial_\nu\Omega - \Omega^{-2}\partial_\mu\Omega\,
\partial_\nu\Omega$. Contracting with $g^{\mu\nu}$: $\Box\ln\Omega = \Omega^{-1}\Box\Omega - (\partial\ln\Omega)^2$, which is the identity.
Multiplied by $-6$ it turns $-6\Omega^{-1}\Box\Omega$ into $-6\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2$.
:::

The round sphere is conformally flat, through the stereographic projection. The second exercise uses the
two-dimensional formula to recover its curvature from flat space.

::: {#exr-kkr-weyl-stereographic}
#### The sphere from the plane

The stereographic metric of the unit sphere is $\Omega^2(dx^2 + dy^2)$ with $\Omega = 2/(1 + x^2 + y^2)$. Compute its
curvature with SageManifolds and with the two-dimensional formula of @exm-weyl-two-dimensions.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $R = 0$ and the flat Laplacian $\Delta$ (the Riemannian $\Box$), $\tilde R = -2\Omega^{-2}\Delta\ln\Omega$, and
$\Delta\ln\Omega = -4/(1 + x^2 + y^2)^2 = -\Omega^2$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-weyl-stereographic >}}

The curvature is $2$, that of the unit sphere.
:::

The coefficients of the formula depend on the dimension. The third exercise checks them for $n = 3$. A conformally flat metric with a one-variable factor suffices.

::: {#exr-kkr-weyl-three-dims}
#### Three dimensions

Check with SageManifolds that $\tilde g = \Omega(x)^2(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)$ has $\tilde R = \Omega^{-2}(-4(\ln\Omega)'' -
2((\ln\Omega)')^2)$, the $n$-dimensional formula with $n = 3$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $n = 3$ the coefficients are $2(n - 1) = 4$ and $(n - 1)(n - 2) = 2$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-weyl-three-dims >}}
:::
::::

### Jordan and Einstein frames

The reduced action can be written with different four-dimensional metrics, related by Weyl rescalings by powers of
$\phi$. The two common choices are named after the forms of the action they produce; the first is the one that comes
directly out of the reduction.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-jordan-frame}
#### Jordan frame

The **Jordan frame** is the description in which the metric is the one appearing in the higher-dimensional
ansatz: the reduced action @eq-kk-reduced-action, $-\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,\phi(R + \tfrac14\phi^2F^2)$, with the
scalar multiplying the curvature. In it the effective Newton constant is $G/\phi$, varying in space and time.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Scalar-tensor theories of gravity were studied independently of Kaluza-Klein theory. The first example places the
Jordan-frame action among them. The comparison fixes the value of the Brans-Dicke parameter.

::: {#exm-jordan-brans-dicke}
#### Brans-Dicke theory

$-\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,(\phi R - \omega\phi^{-1}(\partial\phi)^2)$, with $(\partial\phi)^2 = g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial_\nu\phi$,
is the Brans-Dicke action in the signature $(+, -, -, -)$, and the Kaluza-Klein scalar is the case $\omega = 0$ [@overduin1998, eq. 13]; solar-system tests require $\omega > 500$, so the scalar must be
stabilised by extra ingredients in any realistic model.
:::

The frames differ in which metric measures lengths. The second example asks which one test particles follow. The answer depends on what the particle couples to.

::: {#exm-jordan-geodesics}
#### Which metric do particles follow?

A five-dimensional geodesic projects to a four-dimensional curve that is a geodesic of neither frame in general;
for the charged Kaluza-Klein black hole @duff1994 [p. 10] argues that the Weyl-rescaled metric
$e^{\sqrt3\phi}g_{\mu\nu}$ is the one coupling to a charged particle's worldline. The choice of frame is a matter of
which quantities are held fixed, not of physics [@overduin1998, Sec. 3.7].
:::

The scalar has no kinetic term in the Jordan frame. The third example notes this, which is what the Einstein frame
repairs.

::: {#exm-jordan-sign}
#### No kinetic term

The Jordan-frame action has no $(\partial\phi)^2$ term at all (@exr-kk-total-derivative): the scalar's dynamics is
entirely hidden in its coupling to $R$, and is revealed by the rescaling below.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise reads off the effective gravitational coupling of the Jordan frame. It makes the statement "$G/\phi$"
quantitative. The result is plotted in the figure of the dilaton couplings below.

::: {#exr-kkr-jordan-newton}
#### The effective Newton constant

In the Jordan frame with $A = 0$, read off the coefficient of $\sqrt{-g}R$ in @eq-kk-reduced-action and the effective
Newton constant. By how much does gravity weaken where the circle is twice as large?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The coefficient is $-\frac{2\pi\phi}{2\hat\kappa^2}$, which has the Einstein-Hilbert form $-\frac{1}{16\pi G_{\text{eff}}}$
with $16\pi G_{\text{eff}} = 2\hat\kappa^2/(2\pi\phi)$, i.e. $G_{\text{eff}} = G/\phi$ with $G$ the value at $\phi = 1$. Where the
circle is twice as large ($\phi = 2$) the effective Newton constant is halved: gravity is diluted over a larger
internal volume, the mechanism of @exr-frame-newton applied point by point (@fig-kkr-couplings).
:::

Neutral particles do not feel the gauge field. The second exercise asks which four-dimensional metric they follow
when the circle has varying size.

::: {#exr-kkr-jordan-geodesics}
#### Neutral particles

For $A = 0$, show that a five-dimensional geodesic with $p_y = -\phi^2\dot y = 0$ projects to a geodesic of the
Jordan-frame metric $g$, and that a particle with $p_y \neq 0$ feels the force of @exm-christoffel-upper-spacetime.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$p_y = 0$ means $\dot y = 0$, and the spacetime components of the geodesic equation reduce to $\ddot x^\lambda +
\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu = 0$ with $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu} = \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$ for $A = 0$: a geodesic of $g$, and
since $\hat g(\dot x, \dot x) = g(\dot x, \dot x)$ the affine parameters agree. For $p_y \neq 0$, $\dot y = -p_y/\phi^2$ and the
term $\hat\Gamma^\lambda_{yy}\dot y^2 = \phi\partial^\lambda\phi\,p_y^2/\phi^4$ gives $\ddot x^\lambda + \Gamma^\lambda_{\mu\nu}\dot x^\mu\dot x^\nu = -
p_y^2\phi^{-3}\partial^\lambda\phi = \partial^\lambda(p_y^2/2\phi^2)$. For the spatial components $\partial^i = -\partial_i$, so the force points
down the gradient of $p_y^2/\phi^2$, the square of the Jordan-frame Kaluza-Klein mass (@exr-kkr-mass-einstein-frame):
towards larger circles.
:::

The Kaluza-Klein scalar is a Brans-Dicke field with $\omega = 0$. The third exercise performs the frame change for any
$\omega$, which shows which theories have a healthy scalar.

::: {#exr-kkr-jordan-brans-dicke}
#### Brans-Dicke in the Einstein frame

Rescale $g = \phi^{-1}g^E$ in the Brans-Dicke action of @exm-jordan-brans-dicke and show that, up to a total derivative,
it becomes $\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g^E}(-R^E + (\omega + \tfrac32)(\partial_E\ln\phi)^2)$. For which $\omega$ is the scalar
not a ghost?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $\phi R$ term gives @eq-einstein-frame-identity. For the kinetic term, $\sqrt{-g} = \phi^{-2}\sqrt{-g^E}$ and $g^{\mu\nu} =
\phi g_E^{\mu\nu}$, so $\sqrt{-g}\,\phi^{-1}g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\phi\partial_\nu\phi = \sqrt{-g^E}\,\phi^{-2}(\partial_E\phi)^2 =
\sqrt{-g^E}(\partial_E\ln\phi)^2$. Altogether $-\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\sqrt{-g^E}(R^E - \tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2 - \omega(\partial\ln\phi)^2)$
plus a total derivative. The kinetic term $\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}(\omega + \tfrac32)(\partial\ln\phi)^2$ has the healthy sign in
$(+, -, -, -)$ exactly when $\omega > -\tfrac32$; the Kaluza-Klein value $\omega = 0$ gives $\tfrac32$, as in
@eq-einstein-frame-action.
:::
::::

The Einstein frame is defined by the requirement that the coefficient of the curvature be constant. With
@eq-weyl-curvature this fixes the power of $\phi$ in the rescaling and produces a kinetic term for the scalar.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-einstein-frame}
#### Einstein frame

The **Einstein frame** metric is $g^E_{\mu\nu} = \phi\,g_{\mu\nu}$, that is $g = \Omega^2g^E$ with $\Omega^2 = \phi^{-1}$. By
@eq-weyl-curvature and @eq-kk-volume,
$$
\sqrt{-g}\,\phi R = \sqrt{-g^E}\left(R^E + 3\,\Box^E\ln\phi - \tfrac32\,g_E^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\phi\,\partial_\nu\ln\phi\right),
$$ {#eq-einstein-frame-identity}
and dropping the total derivative the reduced action becomes
$$
\hat S = \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g^E}\left(-R^E + \tfrac32\,g_E^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\phi\,\partial_\nu\ln\phi
  - \tfrac14\phi^3F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}_E\right)
$$ {#eq-einstein-frame-action}
[@overduin1998, eq. 17]: canonical gravity ($-R$, the sign of @eq-einstein-hilbert), a scalar with a positive
kinetic term, and Maxwell's term $-\tfrac14F^2$ with a $\phi$-dependent coupling (@prp-einstein-frame).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The kinetic term comes from the derivative terms of the Weyl formula. The first example traces the factors. Its sign is the important point.

::: {#exm-einstein-frame-kinetic}
#### The kinetic term

$\Omega = \phi^{-1/2}$ gives $\ln\Omega = -\tfrac12\ln\phi$, and the terms $-6\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2$ of
@eq-weyl-curvature become $3\Box\ln\phi - \tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2$; the factors $\sqrt{-g}\,\phi = \Omega^4\phi\sqrt{-g^E} =
\phi^{-1}\sqrt{-g^E}$ and $\Omega^{-2} = \phi$ cancel exactly (@exr-kk-weyl); the overall $-\tfrac{1}{2\kappa^2}$ of the
action then turns $-\tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2$ into the positive kinetic term of @eq-einstein-frame-action, the sign a
scalar must have in the signature $(+, -, -, -)$ (@sec-conventions-indices).
:::

The Maxwell term is Weyl invariant in four dimensions, so it keeps the powers of $\phi$ it had. The second example
counts them.

::: {#exm-einstein-frame-maxwell}
#### The Maxwell term

$\sqrt{-g}\,\phi\cdot\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma} = \phi^{-2}\sqrt{-g^E}\,\phi^3\,\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F_{\rho\sigma}
g_E^{\mu\rho}g_E^{\nu\sigma} = \phi^3\sqrt{-g^E}F^2_E$: the dilaton coupling $\phi^3$.
:::

In the Einstein frame the Newton constant is a constant. The third example relates it to the five-dimensional one. This is the relation that makes gravity weak in four dimensions.

::: {#exm-einstein-frame-newton}
#### Newton's constant

In the Einstein frame the coefficient of $R^E$ is the constant $1/2\kappa^2$ with $\kappa^2 = \hat\kappa^2/2\pi$: the
four-dimensional Newton constant is the five-dimensional one divided by the circumference of the circle,
$G_4 = G_5/2\pi R$ for a circle of radius $R$ [@overduin1998, eq. 10] (@exr-frame-newton).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives the relation between the two Newton constants for a circle of radius $R$. It is the
relation used throughout @sec-kk-tower.

::: {#exr-frame-newton}
#### Newton's constant and the circle

With $\hat S = -\frac{1}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int d^5x\sqrt{|\hat g|}\,\hat R$ and a circle $0 \leq y < 2\pi R$, express the
four-dimensional $\kappa$ in terms of $\hat\kappa$ and $R$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\phi = R$ constant (the circle has circumference $2\pi R$ for $0 \leq y < 2\pi$ in @eq-kk-ansatz) the $y$
integral gives $2\pi$ and the factor $\phi = R$: $\hat S = -\frac{2\pi R}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int\sqrt{-g}\,R_4 + \dots$, so
$\kappa^2 = \hat\kappa^2/2\pi R$, that is $G_4 = G_5/(2\pi R)$: gravity is weaker in four dimensions by the volume of
the internal space, the mechanism of @arkanihamed1998 for large extra dimensions (Part VI). In Duff's
normalisation with $0 \leq my \leq 2\pi$ this is $2\pi\kappa^2 = m\hat\kappa^2$ [@duff1994, p. 5].
:::

The power $\phi^1$ in $g^E = \phi g$ was stated, not derived. The second exercise derives it as the unique power that
makes the coefficient of the curvature constant.

::: {#exr-kkr-einstein-exponent}
#### Why $\phi^1$?

Write $g = \phi^ag^E$ and find the power of $\phi$ multiplying $\sqrt{-g^E}R^E$ in $\sqrt{-g}\,\phi R$. Which $a$ gives the
Einstein frame?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\Omega^2 = \phi^a$: $\sqrt{-g} = \phi^{2a}\sqrt{-g^E}$ and $R = \phi^{-a}(R^E + \dots)$ by @eq-weyl-curvature, so $\sqrt{-g}\,\phi
R = \phi^{1 + a}\sqrt{-g^E}(R^E + \dots)$. The coefficient is constant for $a = -1$, $g = \phi^{-1}g^E$, as in
@def-einstein-frame. In $d$ dimensions the same count gives $\phi^{1 + a(d - 2)/2}$ and $a = -2/(d - 2)$
(@exr-kkr-int-dimension).
:::

The two frames assign different masses to the same particle. The third exercise relates them, which is needed to
compare the Kaluza-Klein masses of @sec-kk-tower in the two frames.

::: {#exr-kkr-einstein-masses}
#### Masses in the two frames

A point particle of mass $m$ in the Jordan frame has action $-m\int d\tau_J$ with $d\tau_J^2 = g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu$. Show
that its Einstein-frame mass is $m\phi^{-1/2}$ for constant $\phi$, and apply this to the Jordan-frame Kaluza-Klein
mass $|n|/(R\phi)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g = \phi^{-1}g^E$ gives $d\tau_J = \phi^{-1/2}d\tau_E$, so $-m\int d\tau_J = -m\phi^{-1/2}\int d\tau_E$: the Einstein-frame mass is
$m\phi^{-1/2}$. For the Kaluza-Klein modes, $|n|/(R\phi) \cdot \phi^{-1/2} = |n|/(R\phi^{3/2})$, which is what the wave
equation gives directly in @exr-kkr-mass-einstein-frame.
:::
::::

In the Einstein frame the scalar has a kinetic term with a non-standard normalisation. Rescaling the field to make it
canonical defines the dilaton, and exposes the exponential coupling to the Maxwell term.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-dilaton}
#### Dilaton

The **dilaton** is the canonically normalised scalar $\sigma = \sqrt3\ln\phi$, in terms of which
@eq-einstein-frame-action reads
$$
\hat S = \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\int d^4x\sqrt{-g^E}\left(-R^E + \tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2 - \tfrac14e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2\right),
$$ {#eq-dilaton-action}
a massless scalar without potential coupled to the Maxwell term through $e^{\sqrt3\sigma}$ [@duff1994, eq. 8, with
$\sigma = -\phi_{\text{Duff}}$].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The coefficient $\sqrt3$ is not a choice. The first example shows that it is forced by the normalisation of the
kinetic term.

::: {#exm-dilaton-normalisation}
#### Fixing the normalisation

$\tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2 = \tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2$ requires $\ln\phi = \sigma/\sqrt3$, and then $\phi^3 = e^{\sqrt3\sigma}$: the
coefficient $\sqrt3$ in the exponent is forced by the kinetic normalisation (@exr-dilaton-normalisation).
:::

The dilaton has no potential. The second example draws the consequence: the size of the circle is undetermined. This is the moduli problem of every compactification.

::: {#exm-dilaton-flat-direction}
#### A flat direction

$\sigma$ has no potential: every constant value is a vacuum, the radius of the circle is a modulus (a flat
direction in the sense of @exm-f-term-flat), and the global shift $\sigma \to \sigma + c$ with $A \to e^{-\sqrt3c/2}A$ is a
symmetry of @eq-dilaton-action [@duff1994, eq. 11]. Stabilising this modulus is the first problem of every
compactification (Part VI).
:::

The exponential coupling is characteristic of dimensional reduction. The third example compares it with other
dilaton couplings. The value of the coupling distinguishes the theories.

::: {#exm-dilaton-black-hole}
#### The dilaton coupling $a = \sqrt3$

Dilaton black holes with $e^{-a\sigma}F^2$ have $a = 0$ for Reissner-Nordström, $a = 1$ for the string dilaton and $a =
\sqrt3$ for Kaluza-Klein [@duff1994, p. 30]; the extreme Kaluza-Klein black holes have the charge-to-mass ratio of
the massive modes of @sec-kk-tower.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
![The couplings of the reduced theory as functions of the size $\phi$ of the circle, with $y \sim y + 2\pi R$: the
Jordan-frame Newton constant $G/\phi$ (blue), the Einstein-frame gauge coupling $e\phi^{-3/2}$ read off from
$-\tfrac14e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2 = -\tfrac14\phi^3F^2$, which coincides with the Einstein-frame mass $m_1R = \phi^{-3/2}$ of the
first Kaluza-Klein mode (red; dashed, the Jordan-frame mass $\phi^{-1}$), and the ratio $q_n/(\sqrt2\kappa m_n) = 1$
(green), independent of $\phi$. The exponents are checked symbolically, the mass from the wave equation on $\phi^{-1}\eta -
\phi^2dy^2$ with SageManifolds. Generated by `figures/kkr_couplings.sage`.](figures/kkr_couplings.svg){#fig-kkr-couplings width=75%}

{{< interactive kkr_couplings 460 >}}

The first exercise derives @eq-dilaton-action from @eq-einstein-frame-action. It is the computation behind
@exm-dilaton-normalisation. Only the normalisation of the kinetic term is needed.

::: {#exr-dilaton-normalisation}
#### The dilaton

Derive @eq-dilaton-action from @eq-einstein-frame-action.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\phi = e^{c\sigma}$, $\ln\phi = c\sigma$ and $\tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2 = \tfrac32c^2(\partial\sigma)^2$, which equals
$\tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2$ for $c = 1/\sqrt3$; then $\phi^3 = e^{3c\sigma} = e^{\sqrt3\sigma}$. The sign of $\sigma$ is a
convention: @duff1994 writes $e^{-\sqrt3\phi}$ with his $\phi = -\sigma$.
:::

The shift symmetry of @exm-dilaton-flat-direction is stated without proof. The second exercise verifies it and
identifies the physical quantity it changes.

::: {#exr-kkr-dilaton-shift}
#### The shift symmetry

Show that @eq-dilaton-action is invariant under $\sigma \to \sigma + c$, $A_\mu \to e^{-\sqrt3c/2}A_\mu$, $g^E$ fixed. How does the
effective gauge coupling of @fig-kkr-couplings change?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R^E$ and $(\partial\sigma)^2$ do not change, and $e^{\sqrt3(\sigma + c)}(e^{-\sqrt3c/2})^2F^2 = e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2$. The symmetry
changes the vacuum value of $\phi = e^{\sigma/\sqrt3}$ by $e^{c/\sqrt3}$ and hence the effective coupling $e\phi^{-3/2}$ by
$e^{-\sqrt3c/2}$, compensated by the rescaling of $A$: in the zero-mode theory the value of the gauge coupling is not
fixed. It is fixed only by the charged massive modes, whose charges $n/R$ are quantised (@def-charge-quantisation),
so the symmetry is broken by the full tower.
:::

The dilaton is sourced by the electromagnetic field. The third exercise derives its field equation and recovers the
constraint of @exm-ricci-yy.

::: {#exr-kkr-dilaton-equation}
#### The dilaton equation

Derive the field equation of $\sigma$ from @eq-dilaton-action. Can $\sigma$ be constant in a Coulomb field?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $L = \tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2 - \tfrac14e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2$, the Euler-Lagrange equation $\nabla^E_\mu(\partial L/\partial(\partial_\mu\sigma)) = \partial
L/\partial\sigma$ gives $\Box^E\sigma = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{4}e^{\sqrt3\sigma}F^2$. A Coulomb field has $F^2 = -2E^2 \neq 0$, so $\Box\sigma
\neq 0$ and $\sigma$ cannot be constant: the electric field sources the dilaton, the Einstein-frame form of the
inconsistency of Kaluza's $\phi = 1$ (@exm-ricci-yy, @exr-kkr-ricci-constant-phi).
:::
::::

The two propositions of this section are the curvature formula and the Einstein-frame identity. The first is the
four-dimensional case of the Weyl formula, and the second rests on it.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-weyl-curvature}
#### The Weyl rescaling formula

In four dimensions $\tilde R = \Omega^{-2}R - 6\Omega^{-3}\Box\Omega$ for $\tilde g = \Omega^2g$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** The `ideal_membership` shape, here closed by `ring` after unfolding, since the inverse metric is
explicit; certificate pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Weyl.weyl_scalar`, for a diagonal metric with arbitrary functions, a polynomial
identity in the jets of $g$ and $\Omega$.

{{< lean KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Weyl.weyl_scalar >}}

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation for general metrics with SageManifolds on de Sitter space with $\Omega(t)$
(`figures/kk_einstein_frame.sage`) and on a static spherically symmetric metric with $\Omega(r)$ (@exr-kk-weyl); the
two-dimensional formula likewise on the sphere.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
De Sitter space is a rescaling of Minkowski space. The first example obtains its curvature from the formula with $R =
0$.

::: {#exm-kkr-weyl-de-sitter}
#### De Sitter from Minkowski

In conformal time $\tau < 0$, de Sitter space is $\Omega^2\eta$ with $\Omega = -1/(H\tau)$. With $R = 0$ and $\Box\Omega =
\partial_\tau^2\Omega = -2/(H\tau^3)$, the formula gives $\tilde R = -6\Omega^{-3}\Box\Omega = -6(-H\tau)^3 \cdot (-2)/(H\tau^3) = -12H^2$,
the curvature of de Sitter space in the signature $(+, -, -, -)$ (@exr-kkr-weyl-de-sitter).
:::

Unlike the reduction formulas, the Weyl formula does not hold with the inverse metric as free symbols. The second
example shows where the relation between $g^{\mu\nu}$ and $g_{\mu\nu}$ enters.

::: {#exm-kkr-weyl-true-inverse}
#### The true inverse is needed

With $g^{\mu\nu}$ free the identity fails, while with the true inverse it holds: the derivation uses $g^{\mu\lambda}g_{\lambda\nu} =
\delta^\mu_\nu$, for instance in $g^{\mu\nu}g_{\mu\nu} = 4$, which produces the coefficient $6 = 2(n - 1)$
(@exr-kkr-jets-free-inverse). For a diagonal metric the inverse is explicit and the issue does not arise.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** `KaluzaKlein.AbelianKK.Weyl.weyl_scalar` avoids the issue with a diagonal metric, whose inverse is
explicit.

**Sage.** `sage/kk_weyl.sage` reports that with $g^{\mu\nu}$ free the identity fails, while at random points with the
true inverse it holds.
:::

The formula is the same in every signature. The third example checks the claim made in the definition. The argument is the one used for the reduction formula in @exr-kkr-scalar-mostly-plus.

::: {#exm-kkr-weyl-signature}
#### Independence of the signature

Under $g \to -g$ (with $\Omega$ fixed), $\tilde g \to -\tilde g$, $R \to -R$, $\tilde R \to -\tilde R$ and $\Box \to -\Box$, so both sides of
$\tilde R = \Omega^{-2}R - 6\Omega^{-3}\Box\Omega$ change sign: the formula of a mostly-plus reference is the same formula,
which is why @eq-weyl-curvature could be quoted from @overduin1998 unchanged.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the formula on a static spherically symmetric metric and then the Einstein-frame
identity. It tests both propositions on the same metric.

::: {#exr-kk-weyl}
#### Weyl rescaling with SageManifolds

Check @eq-weyl-curvature on a static spherically symmetric metric with $\Omega(r)$, and then
@eq-einstein-frame-identity for $g = \phi^{-1}g^E$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kk-weyl >}}
:::

The second exercise verifies @exm-kkr-weyl-de-sitter with SageManifolds. It tests the sign of the curvature as well as
the formula. @exm-weyl-four-dimensions treats a different rescaling of the same space.

::: {#exr-kkr-weyl-de-sitter}
#### De Sitter space

Compute the curvature scalar of $\Omega^2\eta$, $\Omega = -1/(H\tau)$, with SageManifolds and compare with the formula.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
{{< sage exr-kkr-weyl-de-sitter >}}

In the signature $(+, -, -, -)$ de Sitter space has $R = -12H^2$; in the mostly-plus signature the same space has $R = +
12H^2$ (@exm-kkr-weyl-signature).
:::

Rescaling by $\Omega$ and then by $\Omega^{-1}$ must return the original curvature. The third exercise checks this
consistency, which tests the derivative terms of the formula.

::: {#exr-kkr-weyl-inverse}
#### Rescaling back

Apply @eq-weyl-curvature to $g = \Omega^{-2}\tilde g$, using $\tilde\Box f = \Omega^{-2}(\Box f + 2g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\ln\Omega\,\partial_\nu f)$ in
four dimensions, and show that it returns $R$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\ln\Omega^{-1} = -\ln\Omega$: $R = \Omega^2(\tilde R + 6\tilde\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\tilde\partial\ln\Omega)^2)$. Here $\tilde\Box\ln\Omega =
\Omega^{-2}(\Box\ln\Omega + 2(\partial\ln\Omega)^2)$ and $(\tilde\partial\ln\Omega)^2 = \Omega^{-2}(\partial\ln\Omega)^2$, and $\Omega^2\tilde R = R -
6\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2$. Altogether $R - 6\Box\ln\Omega - 6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2 + 6\Box\ln\Omega + 12(\partial\ln\Omega)^2 -
6(\partial\ln\Omega)^2 = R$.
:::
::::

The second proposition is the Einstein-frame identity. Its general proof is the algebra of @exm-einstein-frame-kinetic
applied to @prp-weyl-curvature; it turns the reduced action into the Einstein-frame action.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-einstein-frame}
#### The Einstein-frame identity

@eq-einstein-frame-identity holds for $g = \phi^{-1}g^E$; it follows from @prp-weyl-curvature by the algebra of
@exm-einstein-frame-kinetic.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation with SageManifolds on a static spherically symmetric $g^E$ and $\phi(r)$
(@exr-kk-weyl); the general case follows from @prp-weyl-curvature by the algebra of @exm-einstein-frame-kinetic,
argued in the text.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
For constant $\phi$ the identity is the constant rescaling of @exm-weyl-constant. The first example checks this case. It shows that the Einstein frame is then a mere change of units.

::: {#exm-kkr-einstein-constant}
#### Constant $\phi$

For constant $\phi$, $g^E = \phi g$ has $\sqrt{-g^E} = \phi^2\sqrt{-g}$ and $R^E = \phi^{-1}R$, so $\sqrt{-g^E}R^E = \phi\sqrt{-g}R$,
and the derivative terms vanish: @eq-einstein-frame-identity reduces to an identity between constants, and the
Einstein frame is a change of units by $\sqrt\phi$.
:::

The identity contains a total derivative that disappears from the action. The second example writes it. It is the reason the identity and the action differ by one term.

::: {#exm-kkr-einstein-boundary}
#### The boundary term

$3\sqrt{-g^E}\Box^E\ln\phi = 3\partial_\mu(\sqrt{-g^E}g_E^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu\ln\phi)$ by @exr-kk-total-derivative applied to $g^E$, a
total derivative; the only trace of the rescaling in the action is the kinetic term $-\tfrac32(\partial\ln\phi)^2$.
:::

In cosmology the two frames give different expansion histories. The third example, checked in
@exr-kkr-einstein-frame-frw, states the identity for a homogeneous metric.

::: {#exm-kkr-einstein-frw}
#### A cosmological metric

For $g^E = dt^2 - a(t)^2d\vec x^2$ and $\phi = \phi(t)$, $R^E = -6(\dot a^2 + a\ddot a)/a^2$, $\Box^E\ln\phi = a^{-3}\partial_t(a^3\partial_t\ln\phi)$ and
$(\partial\ln\phi)^2 = (\partial_t\ln\phi)^2$; the identity then expresses the curvature of the Jordan metric $\phi^{-1}g^E$, whose scale
factor is $a/\sqrt\phi$, through these.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise verifies @exm-kkr-einstein-frw with SageManifolds. It is a check of the identity on a family of
metrics different from that of @exr-kk-weyl.

::: {#exr-kkr-einstein-frame-frw}
#### The identity on a cosmology

Verify @eq-einstein-frame-identity for $g^E = dt^2 - a(t)^2(dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2)$ and $\phi = \phi(t)$ with
SageManifolds.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both sides divided by $\sqrt{-g^E} = a^3$ (with $\sqrt{-g} = \phi^{-2}a^3$):

{{< sage exr-kkr-einstein-frame-frw >}}
:::

The sign of the kinetic term decides whether the scalar is physical. The second exercise shows that it is fixed by the
Weyl formula and not by the signature of the circle, while the Maxwell sign is not.

::: {#exr-kkr-einstein-timelike-circle}
#### A timelike circle

Replace the ansatz by $g + \phi^2(dy + A)^2$ in the signature $(+, -, -, -)$ for $g$, so that the circle is timelike.
Using @exr-kkr-scalar-mostly-plus, find the reduced curvature scalar and the signs of the scalar and Maxwell kinetic
terms in the Einstein frame.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Every term of the reduction depends on $\phi^2$, except $\phi^{-1}\Box\phi = \Box\ln\phi + (\partial\ln\phi)^2$, which depends only on
$\ln\phi^2$; so $\phi^2 \to -\phi^2$ gives $\hat R = R - \tfrac14\phi^2F^2 - \tfrac{2}{\phi}\Box\phi$, while $\sqrt{|\hat g|} =
\phi\sqrt{-g}$ is unchanged. The Einstein-frame rescaling acts only on $\sqrt{-g}\,\phi R$, so the scalar kinetic term
keeps its healthy sign, but the Maxwell term becomes $+\tfrac14\phi^3F^2$: the photon is a ghost with negative energy. A
second time direction is excluded for this reason; the spacelike circle is forced.
:::

The Jordan and Einstein metrics of a cosmology have different scale factors. The third exercise relates them and the
corresponding proper times.

::: {#exr-kkr-einstein-scale-factors}
#### Two scale factors

For $g^E = dt^2 - a_E(t)^2d\vec x^2$ and $\phi = \phi(t)$, write the Jordan metric $g = \phi^{-1}g^E$ in the form $d\tau_J^2 -
a_J(\tau_J)^2d\vec x^2$. If the circle shrinks, which scale factor grows faster?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$g = \phi^{-1}dt^2 - \phi^{-1}a_E^2d\vec x^2$, so $d\tau_J = \phi^{-1/2}dt$ and $a_J = \phi^{-1/2}a_E$. If $\phi$ decreases, $\phi^{-1/2}$
increases and $a_J/a_E$ grows: a shrinking circle makes the Jordan-frame universe expand faster than the
Einstein-frame one. The Kasner solution of @exr-kkr-int-kasner is an example, with $a_J \propto \sqrt t$ and $a_E \propto
t^{1/4}$.
:::
::::

## Exercises {#sec-01-kaluza-klein-reduction-exercises}

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The three exercises below combine the three sections of the chapter. The first two follow an exact five-dimensional
vacuum solution through the whole reduction, from the ansatz to the Einstein frame; the third repeats the reduction in
an arbitrary number of dimensions.

::: {#exr-kkr-int-black-string}
#### The Kaluza-Klein black hole

The product of the Schwarzschild metric with a circle, $f\,dt^2 - f^{-1}dr^2 - r^2d\Omega^2 - dw^2$ with $f = 1 - 2m/r$, is a
five-dimensional vacuum solution, the black string. (a) Boost it along the circle, $t = \cosh b\,t' + \sinh b\,w'$,
$w = \sinh b\,t' + \cosh b\,w'$, and read off $\phi$, $A_\mu$ and the Jordan metric $g_{\mu\nu}$ with @eq-kk-components.
(b) Check with SageManifolds that the five-dimensional metric is Ricci flat and that the four-dimensional fields
satisfy the equations of @exm-kkr-ricci-vacuum and of @exr-kkr-action-dilaton-equation. (c) Write the Einstein-frame
metric. (d) Why is the boosted string not the same five-dimensional space as the unboosted one, although the two are
related by a coordinate change?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) With $c = \cosh b$, $s = \sinh b$: $\hat g_{ww} = fs^2 - c^2 = -\phi^2$ gives $\phi^2 = 1 + \frac{2m}{r}s^2$; $\hat g_{tw} =
(f - 1)sc = -\phi^2A_t$ gives $A_t = \frac{2m}{r}\frac{sc}{\phi^2}$; and $g_{tt} = \hat g_{tt} + \phi^2A_t^2 = f/\phi^2$, the other
components being those of Schwarzschild: $g = \phi^{-2}f\,dt^2 - f^{-1}dr^2 - r^2d\Omega^2$, an electric potential and a
scalar that tends to $1$ at infinity. (b) The checks, the dilaton equation in the form $\phi\Box\phi = \tfrac12\Box\phi^2 -
(\partial\phi)^2$ to avoid square roots:

{{< sage exr-kkr-int-black-string >}}

(c) $g^E = \phi g = \phi^{-1}f\,dt^2 - \phi(f^{-1}dr^2 + r^2d\Omega^2)$, with $\phi = (1 + \frac{2m}{r}\sinh^2b)^{1/2}$: the
electrically charged dilaton black hole with coupling $a = \sqrt3$ (@exm-dilaton-black-hole). (d) The boost mixes $t$
with the periodic coordinate $w$, so it is not a globally defined coordinate change on $\mathbb{R}_t \times S^1_w$: the
identification $w \sim w + 2\pi L$ becomes $(t', w') \sim (t' - 2\pi Ls, w' + 2\pi Lc)$. Locally the two metrics are
isometric, globally they are different spaces, which is why the reduction produces a charged black hole from an
uncharged string; the charge is the momentum along the circle, $\propto mcs$.
:::

The second exercise reduces a cosmological solution. It shows the dilaton rolling, the Jordan and Einstein frames
disagreeing about the expansion, and the vacuum equations at work.

::: {#exr-kkr-int-kasner}
#### A Kasner universe with a shrinking circle

The five-dimensional Kasner metric $dt^2 - \sum_it^{2p_i}(dx^i)^2 - t^{2q}dw^2$ is Ricci flat when $3p + q = 1$ and $3p^2 + q^2
= 1$ for $p_1 = p_2 = p_3 = p$. (a) Find the non-trivial solution and identify $\phi$, $A$ and the Jordan metric. (b) Use
@eq-kk-scalar and @eq-kk-ricci to predict $\Box\phi$ and $R$ for it, and check with SageManifolds. (c) Find the
Einstein-frame metric and its scale factor as a function of its proper time. Which kind of matter produces this
expansion in four-dimensional cosmology?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $q = 1 - 3p$ and $3p^2 + (1 - 3p)^2 = 1$ give $12p^2 = 6p$, so $p = \tfrac12$, $q = -\tfrac12$ (the other root $p = 0$, $q = 1$
is flat space in Milne coordinates). Then $\phi = t^{-1/2}$, the circle shrinking, $A = 0$, and $g = dt^2 - t\,d\vec
x^2$. (b) $\hat R_{yy} = \phi\Box\phi = 0$ and $\hat R = R - 2\phi^{-1}\Box\phi = 0$ predict $\Box\phi = 0$ and $R = 0$. (c) $g^E =
\phi g = t^{-1/2}dt^2 - t^{1/2}d\vec x^2$: proper time $\tau = \int t^{-1/4}dt = \tfrac43t^{3/4}$ and $a_E = t^{1/4} =
(3\tau/4)^{1/3}$:

{{< sage exr-kkr-int-kasner >}}

$a \propto \tau^{1/3}$ is the expansion of a flat universe filled with stiff matter, $p = \rho$, which is what a homogeneous
massless scalar is: in the Einstein frame the shrinking circle appears as the kinetic energy of the rolling dilaton,
$\sigma = \sqrt3\ln\phi = -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\ln t$. In the Jordan frame the scale factor is $\sqrt t$ instead
(@exr-kkr-einstein-scale-factors).
:::

The third exercise repeats the chapter in $d + 1$ dimensions. It shows which numbers in the chapter are special to
four dimensions.

::: {#exr-kkr-int-dimension}
#### Reduction from $d + 1$ to $d$ dimensions

Take the ansatz @eq-kk-ansatz with a $d$-dimensional metric $g$. (a) Find $\det\hat g$ and the volume element. (b)
Assuming that @eq-kk-scalar holds in every dimension (the jet computation never uses $d = 4$), write the reduced
action. (c) Find the Einstein-frame rescaling $g = \phi^ag^E$, using the $n$-dimensional Weyl formula of
@def-weyl-curvature-formula. (d) Show that the canonical dilaton is $\sigma = \sqrt{2(d - 1)/(d - 2)}\,\ln\phi$ and that the
Maxwell term becomes $-\tfrac14e^{a\sigma}F^2$ with $a = \sqrt{2(d - 1)/(d - 2)}$. Check $d = 4$. What goes wrong for $d = 2$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
(a) $\det\hat g = -\phi^2\det g$ (@exr-kkr-volume-dims) and $\sqrt{|\hat g|} = \phi\sqrt{|g|}$. (b) $-\frac{2\pi}{2\hat\kappa^2}\int
d^dx\sqrt{|g|}\,\phi(R + \tfrac14\phi^2F^2)$, the $\Box\phi$ term being a total derivative as before. (c) With $\Omega^2 = \phi^a$,
$\sqrt{|g|}\,\phi R = \phi^{ad/2}\phi\,\phi^{-a}\sqrt{|g^E|}(R^E + \dots)$, constant coefficient for $a(d - 2)/2 = -1$: $g =
\phi^{-2/(d - 2)}g^E$. (d) With $\ln\Omega = -\ln\phi/(d - 2)$ the term $-(d - 1)(d - 2)(\partial\ln\Omega)^2$ of the Weyl formula gives
$-\frac{d - 1}{d - 2}(\partial\ln\phi)^2$ inside the bracket, hence the kinetic term $\frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\frac{d - 1}{d - 2}(\partial\ln\phi)^2
= \frac{1}{2\kappa^2}\tfrac12(\partial\sigma)^2$ for $\sigma = \sqrt{2(d - 1)/(d - 2)}\ln\phi$. The Maxwell term picks up $\Omega^{d - 4}$
(@exr-kkr-weyl-maxwell): $\phi^3\phi^{-(d - 4)/(d - 2)} = \phi^{2(d - 1)/(d - 2)} = e^{a\sigma}$ with $a = \frac{2(d - 1)}{d -
2}\big/\sqrt{\frac{2(d - 1)}{d - 2}} = \sqrt{\frac{2(d - 1)}{d - 2}}$. For $d = 4$: $\sigma = \sqrt3\ln\phi$, $a = \sqrt3$ and the
weight $\phi^3$, as in @def-dilaton. For $d = 2$ the exponent $-2/(d - 2)$ is undefined: two-dimensional gravity is
Weyl invariant ($\sqrt g R$ is a total derivative) and no rescaling can remove $\phi$, which survives as a
dilaton-gravity theory.
:::
::::
